children.text: Our estimator carries a new pool screen enclosure as a single $15,000 line, and it shows every total in a band of plus or minus 10 percent. That figure describes a cage designed alongside a new pool and deck, on a site with ordinary access, where the concrete underneath it was poured knowing the cage was coming.

Three things move it from there, and only one of them is the size of your backyard. The cage's height and clear span decide how much aluminum is in it. The wind load your structure is engineered to decides how thick that aluminum has to be and how often it is anchored. And the concrete under the posts decides whether the footings are already in the ground or have to be cut into a finished deck.
That third one is the expensive one, it is invisible in every photograph, and it is the only item on the list that stops being cheap on a specific day: the day the deck sets.
Three prices arriving as one

celdas: Posts, beams, chair rails, fasteners, bracing
Height, clear span, and the load the engineer designs to
Footings, anchors, and the connection to the house
Whether the concrete was poured for a cage, or is being drilled after the fact
Mesh choice, panel width, and how many doors

children.text: Homeowners shop the third line, argue about the first, and rarely ask about the second. The second is where two quotes for "the same cage" actually separate, because it is the only one that never appears in a rendering.
Price follows surface and span, not deck footprint
The screen on a pool enclosure is the roof plus the walls. Your deck footprint sets the roof.
Height sets the walls, on all four sides at once.

Raise a cage two feet over the same deck and you have not added two feet. You have added a band of screen around the entire perimeter, longer posts, and — because those posts are now carrying more load over more distance — a heavier post and beam schedule underneath the whole thing. Height is the single most common reason two enclosures over identical decks are priced well apart.

Clear span does the same work sideways. Every upright you take out of a sightline has to be paid for in a deeper beam. That is the honest trade behind wide-panel and panoramic framing: the view is real, and so is the aluminum it takes to hold the opening. Which one suits the yard is a look-and-feel question. What it costs is an engineering one, and it is settled by where the uprights land — so ask for the post layout on the drawing, not a description of the view.

Roof profile is the third dimension of the same question. A flatter profile carries a shorter span and looks lower from the yard; a steeper one sheds rain and debris more readily and adds height at the ridge, along with everything height brings with it. These are not interchangeable styling options with one price.

blog.alt: Pool and raised spa inside a screen enclosure, with a stone water feature spilling into the pool at one end, lounge chairs and a fire table on the travertine deck, and a lake beyond the mesh.

children.text: The wind load is a property-level number, not a Florida number

A pool enclosure is an engineered structure. Somebody seals drawings for your address, a plan reviewer in your county checks them, and an inspector verifies that what went up matches what was sealed. That sequence is not a formality — it is most of what you are buying when you buy a cage rather than a carport.
Two inputs into those drawings change the aluminum, and both are specific to your lot rather than to the state:
The design wind speed at your address.
It is not uniform across Florida, and it is not uniform across a county either.
The exposure the site actually has.

A lot backing onto open water or a wide lake is not in the same situation as an identical lot screened by two-story houses on three sides. The engineer takes a position on that, and the position shows up as extrusion sizes, anchor spacing and cable bracing.
This gives you the most useful question in the entire comparison, and almost nobody asks it:
what design wind speed and what exposure category was this quote engineered to?
Two bidders who answered that differently have not given you two prices. They have given you two structures. Ask for both figures in writing, on the quote itself.

Be equally direct about what happens afterwards. A cage is a permitted, inspected structure, and it should be permitted under the license of the contractor building it — which you can confirm yourself in the state's public register before signing anything.
What permits are required for pool construction in Florida
covers how the reviews stack up when the pool and the enclosure are happening together.
The footings are the line nobody plans for

The posts do not stand on the deck. They stand on concrete that has to be thick enough and reinforced enough to hold a structure down in wind, and a pool deck poured without a cage in mind is not automatically that concrete.
Which side of this you land on is decided by timing, not by budget.
If the pool and deck are being built now,

the cage is drawn first and the deck is poured to receive it: thickened edges and footings go in while the ground is open and the forms are already set. The incremental cost of doing it in that order is close to nothing, and it is the reason our estimator's $15,000 line is a realistic planning number in a new build.
If the deck is already finished,

the work becomes demolition. Cores get drilled; where the slab turns out to be too thin or unreinforced, sections are cut out, new footings are poured, and the surface is put back. Our estimator prices decking at $12 a square foot for concrete, $22 for pavers and $35 for travertine, which gives you a sense of what is being cut into — and the patch never quite matches the field around it, no matter which of the three it is. Pavers are the forgiving case, because they can be lifted and reset. Poured concrete and travertine are not forgiving.
So the decision that saves the most money here costs almost nothing to make and has to be made early:
if an enclosure is even a possibility, have the deck designed for one.
That belongs on the same list as the other things worth settling while the design is still on paper, in
upgrades worth planning before construction begins
, and next to the questions to answer before any of it starts, in
what to decide before you build a pool in Florida

blog.alt: Curved pool and raised spa under a white-framed screen enclosure, with white Adirondack chairs around a round table on a painted concrete deck and an exterior staircase climbing to the teal-sided upper floor of the house.

children.text: Where it meets the house
Most cages attach to the house along one side, and that joint is where enclosure projects generate their long-term complaints.

The beam at the house normally doubles as a gutter, which means the roof edge above it has to drain into it and the fascia below it has to carry structural load. Whether that detail is straightforward depends on what your roof is made of and what condition the fascia is in, and both are things a bidder should have looked at rather than assumed. Ask directly what happens at the house: where the water goes, what the existing gutter does once the cage is up, and who is responsible if the fascia turns out to be soft.

One related habit worth naming, because it shows up on finished cages constantly: the frame is an engineered structure, not a hanging rail. Fans, lights, televisions, shade cloth and sports hardware all end up bolted to cages, and each of them is load the sealed drawings never saw. If you want any of it, say so before the drawings are sealed. Afterwards it is a modification to an engineered structure.

blog.alt: Screen enclosure meeting the house at a covered lanai with a ceiling fan and a built-in grill island, the paver deck running down to a freeform pool, with a lake and power lines beyond the cage.

children.text: Screen, doors, and the question the county answers

Mesh is normally presented last, as a comfort preference. It is worth moving earlier for one reason that rarely gets explained: tighter weaves stop more insects and more light, and they also pass less air, which means the frame catches more wind. That makes the mesh an engineering input, not a finish. Choose it before the drawings are sealed, and ask what each weave costs you in airflow and view before picking the tightest one on the shelf.

Doors are a count, and the count matters more than the door. Each one is an opening in the structure, hardware, and a place the mesh gets handled every day. Two doors on a cage that needs one is a small permanent expense in a place that takes wear.

Then there is the question that is not yours to answer: whether the enclosure is being counted as the pool's safety barrier. Where it is, the door hardware becomes part of the plan review rather than a preference, and that is settled by the reviewer in your county rather than by the catalogue. Ask your builder which way it is being submitted, and get the answer before the doors are ordered.

If there is an existing cage coming down first, its removal and disposal is a separate line and should appear as one. Whether it needs to come down at all is worth asking before it is assumed: a frame that is still sound and a screen that is finished are two different jobs at two different prices.
Eight lines that make two quotes comparable
Enclosure bids are famously hard to read side by side because most of them describe the result rather than the structure. These make them comparable:
Height at the house and at the far end, and the roof profile.
The design wind speed and exposure category the engineering assumes.
Post and beam sizes, and exactly where the uprights land.
What is assumed about the existing concrete, and what happens if it proves too thin — priced, or a change order.
The connection at the house: gutter detail, fascia condition, and who owns the roof edge.
Mesh type, panel by panel, and whether it was priced before or after the engineering.
Door count, hardware, and whether the enclosure is being submitted as the barrier.
Removal and disposal of the existing cage, if there is one.
None of these are traps. A builder who runs these projects will answer all eight quickly, and the speed of the answers tells you nearly as much as their content — which is most of
how to tell one pool builder from another
The order that keeps this from going wrong
Three decisions, in this sequence:
Whether you want one at all.

A cage changes how the yard looks and how it is used, in both directions, and that trade-off is worth settling before anyone measures. It is also where a screen enclosure gets compared with the alternatives that are not really alternatives: our estimator prices an aluminum pergola at $8,500 and a motorized louvered roof at $18,000, and none of the three does the other's job — the two alternatives are priced out in
what an aluminum pergola costs in Florida
and
what a motorized louvered roof costs
How high and how open.
Height, panel width and roof profile, decided together, because each one moves the other two and all three move the price.
What it stands on.
The deck detail and the footings — which has a deadline, and the deadline is the pour.

Taking those out of order is what produces the two expensive surprises on this kind of project: a finished deck cut open for footings, and a cage redesigned after the drawings were sealed. The order is free. The corrections are not.
If you want to see how we scope one — site walk, exposure, height and span, then the deck detail — that is on the
pool screen enclosures
page, and finished cages from our own jobs are in the
project gallery
. To see the $15,000 line sitting inside a whole backyard budget rather than on its own, the
pool cost estimator
puts it next to the pool, the deck and everything else — and if you are still working out the pool itself,
what a custom pool really costs
is the companion to this one. A
project estimate
starts with the site visit, which for an enclosure mostly means looking at what is behind your lot and what is under your deck.

faq.answer: Our estimator carries a screen enclosure as a single $15,000 line and shows every total in a band of plus or minus 10 percent. That is a planning figure for a cage designed alongside a new pool and deck, on a site with ordinary access. Height, clear span, the engineered wind load and the condition of the concrete under the posts all move it from there.
faq.question: How much does a pool screen enclosure cost in Florida?

faq.answer: Less than people expect. Footprint sets the roof area, but the walls are set by height, and height also drives post and beam sizes. A taller cage over the same deck is a bigger structure in every direction, which is why two enclosures covering identical decks can be quoted well apart.
faq.question: Does a bigger pool deck mean a more expensive cage?

faq.answer: Usually the engineering assumptions rather than the aluminum. Ask each bidder what design wind speed and what exposure category the drawings were engineered to, and where the uprights land. Two quotes engineered to different assumptions are two different structures, not two prices for one.
faq.question: Why are two pool enclosure quotes so far apart?

faq.answer: Yes, but the footings are the variable. The posts need concrete beneath them with adequate thickness and reinforcement, and an existing deck may or may not have it. Where it does not, sections get cut out, new footings are poured and the surface is patched, and the patch rarely matches the field around it.
faq.question: Can a screen enclosure be added to a pool deck that is already finished?

faq.answer: It can. Tighter weaves block more insects and more light, and they also let less air pass, which means the frame catches more wind. Mesh is usually presented as a comfort choice, but it is an input the engineer needs before the drawings are sealed rather than a finish selected at the end.
faq.question: Does the screen mesh I choose affect the structure?

summary: A pool cage is not priced by the size of your deck. Here is the number our estimator uses, the three things that actually move it, and the one that stops being cheap the day the concrete sets.
title: How Much Does a New Pool Screen Enclosure Cost in Florida? What Changes the Scope

children.text: Our estimator prices an aluminum pergola at
. That number comes from the same approved price table the
pool cost estimator
runs on, and it is a real figure for an ordinary structure: one pergola, ordinary post spacing, landing on ground that is ready to take it.

What it is not is a price per pergola. Six decisions move that line, and only one of them is size. The rest are structural, they are all made before anything is ordered, and they are the reason two pergola quotes can carry the same total and describe different buildings.
What the $8,500 line actually is

It is a single line item, not a rate. The estimator does not ask how big the pergola is, the way it asks for pool and deck square footage — it adds one figure when you tick the box. That is a deliberate simplification and it holds for the ordinary case.
Tick it on the estimator's default configuration and the range moves from
to
. Which is the honest way to see a pergola in a backyard project: not as a separate purchase, but as roughly a tenth added to the yard.
Two things that line does
not
include:
The permit.
Our estimator calculates permits and engineering as 9 percent of the pool and deck. The pergola is not in that base.
Anything the pergola is meant to hold.
Fans, lights, screens, a heater, speakers. Those are separate, and what they cost later depends on what was run through the posts before they were closed.
1. Span, not square feet
This is the factor that moves the price most and the one homeowners almost never ask about.

People size a pergola by area. Aluminum is priced by what a beam has to carry across an unsupported distance. Take the same footprint and remove two posts to open one side, and you have not saved two footings — you have doubled the clear span, and the beam depth and the wall thickness of the extrusion both have to go up to carry it.

A structure with a post at every corner and one with a long open side can be identical on a floor plan and different on an order sheet. If you want an open side — because it faces the water, or because a post would land where the table goes — that belongs in the first design conversation, not in a change order after the members are ordered.
2. What it lands on
The pergola is only as cheap as the ground under it. In rough order, from least to most expensive:
A pool project still under construction.
Footings go in before the deck is poured. This is the cheapest moment there will ever be, and it is covered in
the upgrades worth planning before construction starts
An existing concrete slab.
Workable, if it is thick enough and reinforced where the posts land. Sometimes it is, and sometimes the honest answer is a poured pad at each post.
An existing paver deck.
Pavers come up, footings get dug and poured, pavers go back. The work is routine; the cost is the labor of doing a deck twice.
Attached to the house.
Trades footings for a ledger connection, a flashing detail and a wall that can take the load. Whether attached or freestanding is the right layout is
a decision of its own
; as a price factor, it moves money from the ground to the wall rather than removing it.
What the footing work involves in each case, and the point at which it stops being free, is the sequencing question in
the seven pergola decisions that close before construction
. For reading a quote, only one thing has to be settled: which of the four rows above you are in. A contractor who has not asked is pricing a different one.

blog.alt: Gabled aluminum patio cover attached to a stucco house, with a weathered wall lantern beside it and a white PVC fence behind.

children.text: 3. Wind load, which is set by the lot

Every permanent structure in Florida is engineered for a design wind speed, and that speed is set by where the lot sits — not by the state as a whole. A coastal South Florida site carries a stricter requirement than an inland North Florida one, and the practical effect is that the same drawing does not carry from one county to the next. Heavier members, more anchors, deeper footings.
For the quote, this has one clear consequence:
engineering is a real line, and sealed drawings are what the building department reviews.
A price with no engineering in it is a price for a structure nobody has checked. What the permit process itself looks like, county by county, is in
whether you need a permit for a pergola in Florida
4. Fixed slats or operable louvers
This is the largest single fork available, and the estimator prices both sides of it:
for a pergola,
for a motorized louvered roof. The gap is $9,500 — more than the pergola costs.
That money buys moving parts, a motor, controls and a rain path that closes, which changes the structure rather than just the top of it. It is a different build, not an upgrade tier, and
which one you should build

is worth settling before you price either. The mistake to avoid is pricing a pergola, deciding later that you wanted the roof to close, and discovering that the posts and footings were sized for the lighter structure.
5. What runs through the posts

Aluminum posts are hollow, and the wire for lights, fans, retractable screens, a heater or speakers runs inside them and through the footings. Done while the frame is still open, it is a small line: conduit and an electrician's hours.

It is small only once. The same fixtures added afterwards mean surface conduit down a finished post, or a trench across a deck that is already laid — and that second bill lands against the deck, not against the pergola, which is why it never appears in the comparison people think they are making. You do not have to buy the fixtures up front. You do have to leave them somewhere to go.
Which provisions are worth leaving, and why it is settled at fabrication rather than at purchase, is
decision six of the seven that close before construction
. Screens, lights and fans follow the same logic on the sides and overhead:
they are designed into the frame, not added to it

blog.alt: Modern aluminum pergola beside a pool with two black electrical cables left hanging from the frame, waiting for light fixtures.

children.text: 6. Site conditions the estimator does price

Three of them, and all three are checkboxes rather than judgement calls. Two are percentage surcharges on the whole project, which means they move the pergola line even when the condition has nothing to do with the pergola:
Difficult access: 8 percent.

A gate too narrow, a slope, a septic field that cannot be crossed, a tree that stays. Our estimator applies it to the whole project, the pergola line included, so the same pergola that is $8,500 on an open lot is
on that one.
Rock excavation: 12 percent.
The rock is under the pool, not under the pergola — but our estimator surcharges the project total the same way, so the pergola line reads
with it ticked, and
with both. Worth knowing before you read the pergola line on a pool quote as a pergola price.
HOA review: $1,500.
A flat line, and the fee is the easy part. The calendar cost is a board that meets when it meets, and the review normally has to clear before the permit application rather than alongside it.

children.text: How to tell two pergola quotes apart
Two totals within a few hundred dollars of each other usually mean two different buildings. Ask both:
How many posts, and what is the longest clear span?
The answer explains most of the price difference on its own.
What is the wall thickness of the extrusion?
"Aluminum" is not a specification. Two structures of identical dimensions can be built from very different members.
Are engineering and sealed drawings included, or extra?
Who pulls the permit and meets the inspector?
It should be the contractor, under their own license. A contractor asking you to pull an owner-builder permit is transferring the liability for the structure to you.
How does it anchor, and what happens to the existing deck?
Lifting and resetting pavers is normal work; it should also be a line rather than a surprise.
What is roughed in for power, and what is capped for later?
What is the finish warranty, and on what exactly?
The structure, the powder coat and the hardware are usually three separate things. Why aluminum holds up the way it does in this climate — and what it holds up better than — is covered in
aluminum against wood over a Florida decade
When $8,500 is not the question you are asking

If the pergola is going beside a pool, over a kitchen, or in front of a screen room, it is not really a standalone purchase — it is one structure in a backyard that has to be laid out at once, because the footings, the conduit, the drainage and the deck all cross each other underground.

and
the outdoor living design guide
both start from the whole yard rather than from one structure, which is the order the ground actually requires.
What to do with all of this
Run the

plus or minus 10 percent
range built from the same approved price table as every figure above. It is meant to tell you which of your decisions is moving your number, not to quote your project.
Then, for a real figure, the span, the anchoring and the wind design all have to be looked at on site. How that works is on the

project evaluation

faq.answer: Area matters less than the longest unsupported span. Two structures with the same footprint can be priced differently because one has a post at every corner and the other leaves a side open, which forces deeper beams and heavier extrusions. Ask for the span and the post count before comparing sizes.

The difference buys moving parts, a motor, controls and a sealed rain path, which changes the structure rather than just the top of it. Whether that gap is worth it depends on what you want the space to do in the rain.

faq.answer: They can, but the cost depends entirely on whether conduit was run inside the posts and footings while the structure was open. Added afterwards, the wiring is either surface-mounted or trenched, and neither is as clean or as cheap as a sleeve placed before the concrete went in.

children.text: Our estimator carries a custom outdoor kitchen as a single $25,000 line, and it shows every total in a band of plus or minus 10 percent. That is a planning figure for a built-in kitchen on a site where the utilities are already close. It is not a quote, and it is not a rate per foot.

The rate-per-foot part is the useful bit. An outdoor kitchen's price barely tracks how long the counter is. It tracks three other things: how many appliances get cut into it, how far the gas, power and water have to travel to reach it, and whether it ends up under a solid roof. Two kitchens of identical length can be entirely different projects on those three questions — the cover over one of them is priced by the same estimator at $8,500 for a pergola or $18,000 for a louvered roof, before a single appliance is chosen.
So the number to carry into your first meeting is not a total. It is an order of decisions, and it is at the end of this article.
The three budgets, and the one nobody plans for
An outdoor kitchen is three purchases that arrive looking like one.

celdas: Frame, veneer, countertop, doors and drawers
Materials, and how many cut-outs the counter has
Your list, which has no ceiling
Gas, electrical circuits, water supply, drain
Distance, and whether finished hardscape has to be cut

children.text: Homeowners budget the first two. Almost nobody budgets the third, because nothing about it appears in the photograph that started the project. The trench, the conduit, the line from the meter and the circuits in the panel are the part of an outdoor kitchen you never see and never stop paying for if the layout puts them far away.
Price follows cut-outs, not linear feet

Every appliance is a hole with a spec sheet attached. A built-in grill has an exact cut-out width, a required depth, a clearance to combustible material, and a ventilation requirement for the enclosed cabinet underneath it. A drop-in cooler is a second hole and a second circuit. A sink is a hole, a supply line and a drain.

Cabinet with doors and nothing in it is the cheapest foot of outdoor kitchen you will ever buy. So a 14-foot run with one grill and storage is a simpler, less expensive build than a 9-foot run carrying a grill, a side burner, a cooler and a sink — even though the short one looks like less kitchen.
This is why a price quoted per linear foot tells you almost nothing on its own. Ask what it assumes about the cut-outs, and the number either holds up or dissolves.

The largest single step in the price is not a length at all. It is the moment plumbing enters the drawing, because that brings in a trade the grill island never needed. Where that line sits for how you actually entertain is the subject of
a grill island compared with a full outdoor kitchen

blog.alt: L-shaped outdoor kitchen under a white louvered roof with a ceiling fan, with a stainless grill, a refrigerator, drawers and a sink cut into a white stone-clad counter, and tile-roofed houses beyond the fence.

children.text: Lock the appliance list before the masonry starts
Cabinets are built to cut-out dimensions. That makes the appliance list a structural decision disguised as a shopping decision.

Swapping a 36-inch grill for a 42-inch one after the block is laid is not a swap. It is demolition and a rebuild of that section, plus whatever the countertop fabrication has already committed to. The same is true in the other direction: a smaller appliance leaves a gap that has to be filled with something that was never drawn.

The rule that avoids all of it is simple and almost nobody follows it: have every appliance specified by model number — ideally sitting on site — before the frame goes up. What goes into that list, and in what order, is covered in
nine decisions to make before you choose appliances

The list is also the second-biggest reason two quotes for "the same kitchen" differ by thousands. One includes an appliance package; the other says appliances by owner. Until you know which, you are comparing a kitchen with a cabinet.
How far the utilities have to travel
Gas, electric, water and drain are four separate runs, each with a length, and the length is the price: trench, conduit or pipe, and a connection at both ends.
Two things make the distance cost more than the distance suggests.
Finished hardscape in the way.

A run that crosses a poured or set deck is a saw cut and a patch. Our estimator prices travertine decking at $35 a square foot, pavers at $22 and concrete at $12, which gives you a sense of what is being cut — and a patched line through any of them never quite matches the field around it.
Panel capacity.

A kitchen with refrigeration, an ice maker, receptacles and lighting can want more dedicated circuits than a house has spare. When the panel is full, a subpanel or a service upgrade becomes a real line item that has nothing to do with the kitchen you were picturing.

Distance is the variable on this list you control most directly, and you control it at the layout stage rather than at the quote stage. A kitchen set fifteen feet closer to the house is the same kitchen with shorter runs. What that costs you is in the sightlines and the traffic pattern, which is a layout question rather than a price question —
designing the layout around the way you actually cook
is where to settle it, and
what gas, electric and plumbing an outdoor kitchen needs
covers what is being run.
The drain is where sinks get decided

A sink needs somewhere for the water to go, and where that is depends on your lot, your existing plumbing and what the local code official accepts. It is a question for a plumber, not for a designer with a rendering.

Some sites answer it in a few feet. Some do not answer it cheaply at all. If yours is the second kind, the honest options are a cold-water prep sink with a simpler disposal path, or no sink — and both are better decisions made on paper than discovered during the trench.
Covered or open changes the number twice

First, the cover is its own project with its own price. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a louvered roof at $18,000. Against a $25,000 kitchen line, that is roughly a third again, or roughly three-quarters again, on top — before anything about the kitchen itself changes.

Second, it changes the kitchen. A built-in grill under a solid roof brings ventilation into the scope: a hood and a path for the air to leave, plus clearances that open sky does not require. An open-slat pergola is a different situation from a solid roof, and the two get quoted differently even when they look similar in a rendering.
Which way to go is a comfort and a use question, and it also decides the specification:
what survives Florida outdoors depends on how exposed the island is
. The narrow point here is that it has to be answered
before
the kitchen is priced, because it changes what is being priced.

blog.alt: Outdoor kitchen on a covered lanai under a solid white roof, with a black granite counter over a white stucco base, a built-in stainless grill, a stainless under-counter door and a travertine floor.

children.text: If there is any chance of a kitchen later, stub it now
This is the single decision in this article most likely to save real money, and it costs almost nothing to make.

If a pool, a deck or a landscape project is happening on the property, the ground is already open and the slab is not yet poured. A gas sleeve, a conduit, a water line and a capped drain run out to where a kitchen might one day go cost a fraction of what the same four runs cost later through finished hardscape — and if the kitchen never happens, you have buried four inexpensive lines.
Doing the reverse is where the surprise bills come from. It belongs on the same list as the other things worth deciding while the design is still on paper, in
upgrades worth planning before construction begins
Where the rest of the money goes

The difference between the low end and the high end of the build itself is mostly in the parts that do not photograph: what the frame is made of, what sits behind the veneer, the countertop, and the doors and drawers.

In Florida the question for each of those is not how it looks on day one. It is what it looks like after ten summers of humidity and UV, and — within a few miles of the coast — salt air. Hollow doors, unsealed substrates and framing that holds moisture fail from the inside, which means the kitchen looks fine right up until it does not. That trade-off, material by material, is
the best outdoor kitchen materials for Florida heat, humidity and rain

blog.alt: Poolside outdoor kitchen under a dark-framed cover, with a domed stainless oven and its chimney on the back counter, a built-in grill and side burners, and a front island with a sink and wood-grain cabinet fronts.

children.text: Seven lines to make a quote show you
Two outdoor kitchen quotes are comparable only when these say the same thing:
The appliance list by model number, and who is buying them.
Countertop material and thickness, and whether any overhang is supported.
The number of dedicated circuits, and whether the existing panel has room.
Gas: natural or propane, line size, and who runs it from the meter or the tank.
Water supply and — specifically — where the drain goes.
Whether the price assumes an existing slab, and what happens if it turns out to be too thin.
The exclusions, written down.
None of those are gotchas. A builder who has run these projects will have the answers ready, and the ones who do not will tell you that by how long it takes them.
The order that keeps this from going wrong
Three decisions, in this sequence:
Where it goes
— relative to the gas meter, the electrical panel, the water, and whatever will cover it.
What is in it
— the appliance list, by model, before anything is built.
What it is made of
— frame, veneer, counter, doors.

Nearly every expensive surprise on an outdoor kitchen comes from taking those out of order: a finished deck cut open for a gas line, a cabinet rebuilt around a grill that changed, a countertop template redone because the sink moved. The order is free. The corrections are not.
If you want to see how we scope one — site walk, utility distances, appliance list, then materials — that is on the
custom outdoor kitchens
page, and finished kitchens from our own jobs are in the
project gallery
. To see the $25,000 line sitting inside a whole backyard budget, the
pool cost estimator
puts it next to the deck, the cover and the rest. And a
project estimate
starts with the site visit, which for a kitchen mostly means measuring how far it is to the meter and the panel.

faq.answer: Our estimator carries a custom outdoor kitchen as a single $25,000 line and shows every total in a band of plus or minus 10 percent. That is a planning figure for the kitchen itself on a site where the utilities are already close. The appliances you select, the distance the gas, power and water have to run, and any structure built over it are separate decisions with separate costs.
faq.question: How much does an outdoor kitchen cost in Florida?

faq.answer: Less than most people expect. The price follows the number of appliance cut-outs and the length of the utility runs rather than the length of the counter. Removing four feet of cabinet with doors saves far less than removing the sink that sits in it.
faq.question: Does a shorter counter make an outdoor kitchen cheaper?

faq.answer: Usually the appliances and the utilities, not the cabinet. Check whether each quote lists the appliances by model and says who buys them, how many dedicated circuits it assumes, and where it says the drain goes. Two quotes only compare once those lines say the same thing.
faq.question: Why are two outdoor kitchen quotes so far apart?

faq.answer: The gas and electrical work is permitted, inspected work, and which office reviews it depends on your county rather than on Florida generally. Have it permitted and inspected under a licensed contractor's license, and confirm that license yourself in the state's public register before you sign.
faq.question: Do I need a permit for an outdoor kitchen?

faq.answer: Yes, but the utility runs cost more once the deck is poured, because reaching the kitchen means saw-cutting and patching finished hardscape. If a kitchen is even a possibility, have the gas, power, water and drain stubbed to the spot while the ground is still open.
faq.question: Can I add an outdoor kitchen after the pool and deck are finished?

children.text: Outdoor living space adds value to a Florida home when four things are true: the work was permitted, the materials survive the climate, the space is usable most of the year, and the design fits the house. When those hold, a pool, a covered lanai, a pergola or an outdoor kitchen is something a buyer will pay for and an appraiser can support. When they do not, the same features are a liability a buyer prices down.

You will see percentages online for how much a pool or a lanai "adds." We do not publish them, because none of them apply to your house: value comes from recent comparable sales in your neighborhood, and a figure that is true in one Boca Raton subdivision is false in a Gainesville one. What we can tell you is what the people who set the value actually look at.
What a buyer sees
Buyers in Florida are evaluating a lifestyle, and the backyard is where it happens. The features that register:
A pool that looks cared for.
Finish, tile and equipment in good condition read as "move-in ready"; a stained, dated pool reads as a project with a cost attached. This is why a
complete remodel
before listing changes how a home shows.
Covered, screened space.
Shade and insect protection are what make a Florida patio usable at 5 p.m. in July. A lanai, a
screen enclosure
or a
pergola
that connects to the house extends the living area in a way buyers feel immediately.
An outdoor kitchen that is part of a room
, not a grill on a slab. Counter space, a sink, lighting and cover.
A layout that flows
from the kitchen or living room to the patio to the pool, without a fence or a step in the wrong place.

blog.alt: Hardwood deck stepping down from a house toward a pool, with planting along the edge.

children.text: What an appraiser sees
An appraiser is comparing your home to recent sales of similar homes nearby and adjusting for differences. For outdoor improvements the questions are:
Was it permitted?
Permitted square footage and structures can be counted; unpermitted work often cannot, and can be flagged.
Is it a durable improvement or a temporary one?
A built pool, a roofed lanai and a masonry outdoor kitchen are improvements. Furniture, portable features and above-ground installations generally are not.
Do comparable homes have it?
In a neighborhood where most homes have a pool, yours is expected and its absence is the adjustment. Where few do, the pool is a smaller adjustment than its cost.
Condition.
A dated or damaged feature can be adjusted down, not up.
The practical consequence: keep the permits, the plans and the closed inspection records with the house. They are the documents that let an improvement count.
What an insurer and the tax office see

A pool and permanent structures are reported to the county property appraiser when they are permitted, and they can change the assessed value. How Florida's homestead rules and assessment caps treat the change depends on your situation; the county property appraiser's office and a tax professional are the right sources, not a blog. Insurers price pools, screened structures and outdoor kitchens by their own underwriting; a conversation with your carrier before you build avoids surprises, and a permitted, code-compliant barrier is usually part of what they want to see.

blog.alt: Outdoor kitchen island with a built-in grill and stone cladding, under a covered patio beside palms.

children.text: What holds value in the Florida climate
Materials decide whether the space still looks like an asset in year ten.

celdas: Travertine, pavers on a proper base, properly finished concrete
Thin overlays, untreated wood at the water's edge
Aluminum pergolas and louvered roofs engineered for the local wind design
Undersized timber structures without footings or hardware rated for wind
Masonry or framed islands with weather-rated appliances and a cover
Aluminum framing and screen rated for the exposure
Repaired-every-year mesh on a frame that was never sized for wind
Finishes chosen for the water chemistry, marine-grade metals
Metals that corrode in salt air or salt water

children.text: Our
outdoor living design guide
goes deeper on materials, and
what makes a pool look custom
covers the design choices that read as quality.
Design that fits the house

The improvements that add the most are the ones that look like they were always there. A pergola scaled to the elevation of the house, a deck material that matches the interior floor tone, a kitchen placed where the cook can see the pool, a screen enclosure whose roof line follows the house. Oversized, mismatched or awkwardly placed features are the ones buyers mentally budget to remove. Planning the pool and the structures together is how you avoid it; our guide to
a pergola beside a pool
is one example of what that planning looks like.

blog.alt: Glass-topped aluminium pergola beside a pool, with a slatted privacy screen at one end.

children.text: A practical order of operations
Decide how you live outside: dining, lounging, swimming, cooking, watching children. The space should serve that, not a listing photo.
Check the rules first: setbacks, easements, HOA, and what needs a permit.
Build the durable elements before the decorative ones: drainage, the pool, the roof or pergola structure, the utilities for a kitchen.
Choose materials for the climate, then for the look.
Keep every permit and inspection record.
If you are weighing a project with resale in mind, we will tell you which parts of it tend to hold value and which are personal preference. Start with a project evaluation on our
custom pool construction
page if the pool is the centerpiece, or with our
outdoor kitchen
and
custom deck
pages for the rest of the backyard.

cardTitle: Outdoor Living and Property Value in Florida

faq.answer: There is no reliable percentage that applies to your house. The value a pool adds depends on the neighborhood, whether comparable homes have pools, the pool's condition and whether it was permitted. In pool-heavy Florida markets a home without one can be at a disadvantage; in others a pool is a preference, not a premium. An appraiser compares your home to recent sales nearby, not to a national average.
faq.question: How much value does a pool add to a house in Florida?

faq.answer: Yes. Unpermitted structures, electrical and gas work surface during inspections, appraisals and insurance underwriting, and can require after-the-fact permits or removal. Keep the permits and the closed inspection records with the house documents.
faq.question: Does unpermitted outdoor work hurt resale?

faq.answer: The one that fits how you live and the house you have. A covered, screened space that is usable in rain and bugs gets the most use in Florida, and a pool is the feature buyers in many markets expect. An outdoor kitchen adds value when it is part of a coherent covered space rather than a grill on a slab.
faq.question: Which outdoor feature is the best investment?

faq.answer: Permitted improvements are reported to the property appraiser and can change the assessed value; how that interacts with Florida's homestead rules depends on your situation, so ask the county property appraiser or a tax professional. Insurers price pools and structures by their own rules; confirm with your carrier before building.

children.text: Most people choose a pool builder by collecting three quotes and picking the middle one. That compares prices, which is the one thing about a pool project that is easy to compare and the least predictive of how it goes.
These are the ten questions worth asking instead. None of them are gotchas — a good builder will have quick, specific answers, and the speed of the answer tells you nearly as much as its content.
The three that matter most
If you only ask three:
Is the license held by the company I am contracting with, and does it cover pool construction?
Who runs my job day to day, and how do I reach them?
How are changes priced and approved once work has started?
Licensing tells you whether the work can be permitted and inspected. The second tells you what the next few months feel like. The third is where most disputes actually begin.
1. What license do you hold, and in whose name?
Pool construction in Florida is a licensed trade with its own classification. A general contractor's license is not the same thing.

Ask for the number, then check it yourself on the state's public lookup. Two things to confirm beyond "active": that the classification covers pool and spa work, and that the name on the license matches the entity on your contract. Work sold by one company and permitted under another's license is a real pattern, and it is the homeowner who is left holding it.
2. Who is actually on my job?
There is a difference between the person who sells the project and the person who runs it. Ask who that second person is, how many jobs they carry at once, and how you reach them.
A specific answer — a name, a phone number, a normal response window — is a good sign. "Someone will always get back to you" is not an answer.

blog.alt: Raised spa with a spillway returning to the pool, framed by a travertine deck beside a single-storey home.

children.text: 3. Is this quote the same scope as the others?
Two pool quotes are almost never for the same thing. One includes the equipment pad relocation, another does not. One assumes standard access, another has walked the side gate.

Put them side by side and compare line by line, not total by total. Where one is silent, ask what happens if that item turns out to be needed. A builder who says "that would be a change order" is being straight with you; the number to be suspicious of is the one with no line items at all.
The decisions that move the price are covered in
what a custom pool really costs
— worth reading before the comparison, so you know which lines to look for.
4. What is not included?

Ask directly. The honest list usually contains some of: utility relocation, unexpected rock, dewatering a high water table, HOA submissions, landscape restoration outside the work area, and the electrical service upgrade a heater sometimes needs.
None of those are red flags as exclusions. They are red flags as surprises.
5. How do change orders work?
The answer you want: in writing, priced, signed before the work happens.

Verbal changes that appear on the final invoice are the most common source of pool disputes, and the fix is entirely procedural. Agree at the outset that nothing changes without a signed order, and the rest of the project gets easier.
6. What does the payment schedule track?

Payments should follow completed stages, not the calendar. A schedule tied to inspected milestones means you are never far ahead of the work and the builder is never funding your job out of the next one.
Be careful with large deposits before anything is permitted, and with a schedule where the final payment is too small to matter — the last 5% is what gets the punch list finished.
7. Who pulls the permits?

The contractor should, under their own license. A builder who asks the homeowner to pull an owner-builder permit is transferring the liability for the work to you, and most people who agree to it do not realize that is what happened.
Permits also tell you about scope: pool, electrical, plumbing and any enclosure or barrier are separate reviews.
What permits are required for pool construction in Florida
covers what a full set looks like.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a pool and raised spa on a travertine deck, with a garden hose coiled at the edge of the lawn.

children.text: 8. What happens if an inspection fails?
Failed inspections happen. The useful question is what the process is when one does — who reschedules, how quickly, and whether the delay is absorbed or billed.
A builder who says inspections never fail is telling you either that they do not do many, or that they are managing your expectations rather than the project.
9. What is the warranty, and on what exactly?

A pool has several different warranties layered on top of each other: the shell, the interior finish, the equipment (manufacturer, not builder) and the labor. They have different lengths and different exclusions.
Ask for them separately and in writing. "Fully warrantied" as a single phrase covers nothing you can rely on later.
10. Can I talk to someone whose pool you finished two years ago?

Anyone can supply a reference from last month. The interesting call is with a customer far enough past completion to have had something go slightly wrong, because the answer you are listening for is how it was handled.
Ask that customer one question: when you called about something after the final payment, what happened?
A note on comparing

It is tempting to treat this as a scorecard. It is more useful as a conversation. What you are really assessing is whether the answers are specific, whether they are consistent across the meeting, and whether the person answering seems to expect the question.
The builder who has thought about failed inspections, exclusions and change orders before you asked is the one who has run enough projects to have needed a process.
If you want to see how our process is structured — from site review through permitting to the punch list — that is on the
custom pool and spa construction
page, and a
project estimate
starts with the site visit rather than a number.

faq.answer: Through the state licensing authority's public lookup, using the license number the contractor gives you. Check that the license is active, that it covers pool and spa construction rather than general contracting alone, and that the name on it matches the company you are contracting with — not an affiliated one.
faq.question: How do I check a Florida pool contractor's license?

faq.answer: Not by itself. The problem is a bid that is lower because it covers less. Two quotes are only comparable when they list the same scope, so the useful exercise is putting them side by side line by line rather than comparing totals.
faq.question: Is the lowest bid usually the problem?

faq.answer: In writing, priced, and signed before the work happens. A verbal change that appears on the final invoice is the single most common source of disputes, and the fix is procedural rather than adversarial: agree at the start that nothing changes without a signed order.
faq.question: What should a change order look like?

faq.answer: Payments should track progress rather than arrive ahead of it. A schedule tied to completed, inspected stages protects both sides — you are never far ahead of the work, and the contractor is never far behind on materials.

children.text: A motorized louvered roof is worth it when it converts hours the space is currently unusable into hours you will actually use it. It is not worth it when it covers ground the house already covers, or when the only thing it is solving is rain. Between them, those two cases account for most of the louvered roofs we are asked to price and then end up talking somebody out of.

Our estimator prices a motorized louvered roof at $18,000 and an aluminum pergola at $8,500. The $9,500 between them does not buy more cover. It buys control: the same structure being open sky at nine, full shade at two, and a closed roof at four. Whether that control is worth $9,500 in your backyard is a question about your backyard, not about the product, and it can be answered in an afternoon without talking to anyone.
First, find the line your house already throws

A great many Florida homes were built with a covered lanai under the main roof. That changes the question completely. You are almost never deciding between cover and no cover. You are deciding whether to extend the usable footprint past the roofline the builder gave you.

So go out at the hour you actually use the yard — for most households that is somewhere between four and seven — and mark where the house's shade ends. Chalk, a hose, a row of chairs, anything. That line is the only measurement that matters at this stage.

Everything inside the line is already covered at the hour you care about. A louvered roof there changes very little, and we see it built there more often than anywhere else, usually because the posts are easier to set against the existing structure and the drawing looks tidy. Everything outside the line is the area where a roof creates usable space that does not exist today. That is what you are buying.
Two things distort the line and are worth checking before you trust it:
The shade moves through the year.
The line you mark in June sits much closer to the house in January. Mark it twice if you can, or at least understand which way it travels.
Low sun goes under a roof, not through it.

Past about five, the sun comes in from the side. A roof — any roof — does nothing about that. The fix is a vertical one: a solid end panel, or a motorized screen planned into the structure rather than added later, which is one of
the features worth comparing before you buy
Second, name the hours out loud
The honest version of "is it worth it" is arithmetic, and it is arithmetic only you can do.

Count the occasions in a normal year when the yard would have been used and was not, and you know why: it was too hot at five, it rained at six, the table was in full sun, the furniture was wet from the morning. Not a feeling — a number you would defend, because it is the only input in this calculation that nobody can supply for you.

Now put $9,500 against that number across the years you expect to own the house. Thirty occasions a year over ten years is three hundred afternoons; twelve a year is a hundred and twenty. Neither number tells you the answer, but both turn a vague want into something you can weigh against the other thing that $9,500 buys in the same backyard.

This exercise is also the fastest way to discover that the answer is a different product. If every occasion on your list is rain, you are describing a fixed cover, which sheds water for less money and has nothing to service. If every occasion is heat at five, you are describing a screen or an end panel.
The full comparison between a pergola, a louvered roof and a fixed panel cover
walks the three of them against each other. The motor is worth paying for when your list has occasions of both kinds on it, because that is the only case where one structure has to do two jobs.

blog.alt: Dark bronze-framed louvered roof with pale blades tilted partly open, seen from underneath against a blue sky, in front of a modern glass-walled house with a black pool fence and clipped hedges.

children.text: Which way the blades run decides whether the motor solves your problem
This is the detail that separates a louvered roof that earns its price from one that disappoints the owner on a schedule.

The blades rotate on one axis. Closing them toward the west blocks low western sun; closing them toward the east does not. If the blades run the wrong way for your yard, rotation gives you bars of light across the table at the exact hour you wanted shade, and no amount of remote-pressing fixes it. The motor is working perfectly. The geometry is wrong.
The problem is that the blade direction is not a free choice. It is traded against two other things at design time:

celdas: What also depends on the blade direction
Why it pulls the other way
Blades span between beams. Running them the way the sun needs can mean a longer span, a deeper beam, or an extra post in the middle of the space.
A closed roof drains to the perimeter beam and down a post. Turn the structure and the low point moves, which can put the discharge somewhere that does not drain.

children.text: None of that is a reason to accept the wrong orientation. It is a reason to raise it early, while it is still a line on a drawing. The question to ask whoever is quoting the job is not "which way do the louvers run" but
"show me where the shade falls at five in the afternoon in July, and where the water comes out."
A good answer arrives immediately and in plain terms. If the shade study is at noon, it is answering a question you did not ask.
What sits underneath moves the answer more than the roof does
A roof over four chairs and a roof over an outdoor kitchen are the same product in two different projects.

Our estimator prices a full outdoor kitchen at $25,000. Appliances, cabinetry and stone that are permanently outside age differently depending on whether they spend the wet season getting rained on, and the roof stops being a comfort item and starts being part of how that installation is specified. The same is true of a television, of upholstered furniture, and of anything with a power outlet in it.

The sequence matters here more than most people expect. Deciding to cover a kitchen after the kitchen is built usually means posts landing where the counter already is. Deciding both at once means the posts, the circuits, the lighting and the drainage are laid out together, and the wiring runs inside the hollow beams instead of on the surface of them. That is the whole argument for planning the structure and its contents in one pass, which is what
designing the lights, fans and screens as one system
is about, and
what an outdoor kitchen actually costs
covers the other half of that budget.

blog.alt: Louvered roof with two ceiling fans over a wood deck, gray lounge furniture in front and a built-in grill island with bar stools and a tall stucco chimney behind, a barrel tile roof showing through the palms.

children.text: Five cases where it is not worth it
The area is already under the lanai at the hour you use it.
Covered in full above, and it is the most common one by a distance.
Rain is the only item on your list.

A fixed solid or translucent cover sheds water, costs less, and has no motor, no dedicated circuit and no actuators. You give up the sky. If you were never going to open it, you were not giving up anything. What a closed louvered roof actually does in a Florida storm is in
rain, wind and what happens to a louvered roof
The space is used almost entirely after dark.
Shade control is worth nothing at nine at night. Lighting, fans and screens are what change that space, and they cost a fraction of the structure.
Nobody in the house is going to touch the control.

This is a real pattern and nobody warns you about it. Some households set the blades once, in the position that is right most of the time, and never move them again. That is a perfectly good outcome for a fixed structure and an expensive way to buy one. If you already know that is your household, say so out loud before you sign.
You are selling inside a couple of years.
Buy it to use it. How buyers price finished outdoor space varies enough by house and neighborhood that no one can honestly hand you a percentage. If the space still needs covering,
what an aluminum pergola costs in Florida
is the more defensible spend on a short horizon.
Three cases where it clearly is
A kitchen, a bar or a television sitting beyond the lanai line.
Something with a cost and a service life is outside the area the house protects. The roof is now part of protecting it.
A west-facing yard used between four and seven.
This is the case the motor was built for: the sun moves, the blades move with it, and a fixed structure cannot follow.
One space that has to be two things across the year.

Sun on the table in February and deep shade in July are opposite requirements. A fixed cover picks one and lives with it. This is the only requirement that a fixed cover genuinely cannot meet, and it is the cleanest reason to pay for the motor.

blog.alt: White louvered roof attached to a two-story house over a poolside patio, the pavers still wet after rain, with the pool edge in the corner, a white fence and a roof with solar panels behind.

children.text: The part that decides how you feel about it in year six

The aluminum and the powder coat will outlast the electronics. Motors, actuators, controllers, rain sensors and the seals between the blades are serviceable parts, and serviceable means that one day they need service.
That is not an argument against the system. It is an argument for asking three specific questions of whoever installs it, before rather than after:
Who services this system locally, and are they you or a third party?
How long do replacement parts take to arrive, and are they stocked in Florida?
How many actuators does this layout use, and what happens to the roof if one fails?

The answer to the second question is what turns a failed actuator into a short inconvenience or a whole season without the roof you paid for, and it predicts your satisfaction in year six better than any feature on a brochure.
The rest of the questions worth asking an installer
go through the contract, the permit and the warranty in the same spirit.

One item specific to here: blade seals and the drainage channels in the beams have to be kept clear of leaf litter. Under live oaks that is not optional, and it is a short job a few times a year that somebody has to actually do.
Deciding this week, without a quote
Mark the shade line at the hour you use the yard. Stand behind it and look at the area beyond it. That is the project.
Write the list of occasions you lost last year and read it back. Rain only, heat only, or both?
Decide what is going underneath, now, even if it gets built in a later phase. Posts and circuits are cheap to move on paper.
Ask for the five-in-the-afternoon shade answer and the water discharge answer from anyone who quotes it.

If the list comes back mixed, the area beyond the line is real, and something with a plug is going under it, the motor earns its price and the remaining question is scope rather than principle — which is what
the seven factors that move a louvered roof's price
are about.

If the list comes back all rain, or the line sits past where you were planning to build, you have just saved yourself the most expensive kind of mistake in this category: the one that works exactly as advertised and still does not get used.
Our
motorized louvered roof systems
page shows how the structures are built and anchored,
the gallery
has finished ones in real North and South Florida backyards, and a
project estimate
starts with walking that shade line with you rather than with a number over the phone.

cardTitle: Is It Worth It in Florida?

faq.answer: It is worth it when you need the same space to be different at different hours and different months: open in February, shaded in July, closed during a storm. If you only need the space to stay dry, a fixed solid or translucent cover does that for less and has nothing to service.
faq.question: Is a motorized louvered roof worth the money over a fixed patio cover?

faq.answer: Treat it as something you buy to use, not as a return. Buyers price finished outdoor space differently depending on the house, the neighborhood and how the work was permitted, so nobody can promise you a number. If you are selling within a couple of years, that alone is a reason to think twice.
faq.question: Does a louvered roof add value to a Florida home?

faq.answer: Over ground the house already covers. Many Florida homes have a lanai under the main roof, and a roof built tight against it often ends up shading a strip that was already shaded at five in the afternoon. The value is in the area beyond that line.
faq.question: Where is a louvered roof usually wasted?

faq.answer: The aluminum structure and the finish outlast the moving parts. Motors, actuators, controllers and blade seals are serviceable items that eventually need service, so the question that predicts your experience is who services the system locally and how long replacement parts take to arrive.
faq.question: How long does a motorized louvered roof last before it needs work?

children.text: Closed, a louvered roof is a roof. The blades overlap, the perimeter beams collect the water, and a post carries it to the ground. Open, it is a frame that wind passes between. Which of those two structures it is when the weather arrives is the whole answer — and the two kinds of Florida weather want opposite positions. The afternoon thunderstorm wants it closed. A named storm wants whatever the manufacturer of that specific system specifies, which is usually open, and which a rain sensor will quietly undo for you if nobody planned for it.
Everything below is the consequence of that. Where the water goes, why the wind rating is two numbers instead of one, and the five things worth getting in writing before the first season.
Rain: the blades are the easy part
With the blades rotated shut, the panels interlock and the roof sheds water. That part works, and it is the part every brochure shows.

What it sheds, it then has to move. The path has four stages: the blade sends water to the perimeter beam, the beam works as a gutter, one or more posts work as downspouts, and the water leaves at the base of a post onto something. Only the first stage is about the roof. The other three are about your yard, and they are where a louvered roof either was designed for the site or was dropped onto it.
Two hundred gallons, roughly

Take a 16-by-20 structure — a normal size over a dining table and a seating group. That is 320 square feet. An inch of rain on 320 square feet is about 200 gallons. That is arithmetic, not a specification, and an inch of rain inside an hour is an ordinary Florida afternoon.
So the useful version of the drainage question is not "does it drain?" It is:
200 gallons has to leave the foot of a post in about the time it took to fall — where does it land, and where does it go from there?
"It drains through the post" is not an answer. These are answers:
It discharges at the northeast post into the existing yard drain.
It discharges onto the paver deck, which falls away from the house toward the swale.
It ties into a pipe run under the new sod to daylight at the back of the lot.

And these are the three outcomes we get called about when nobody asked: a planting bed washed out from underneath, a permanently soft corner of lawn, and a discharge point on the side of the slab that happens to fall back toward the house. None of those are roof failures. All three were decided the day the post positions were set.
Get the discharge point drawn on the plan before construction, with the direction of fall marked. It is one line, and it is the single most useful line on the drawing.

blog.alt: Louvered roof with a dark bronze frame and white blades reaching out over the paved entry court of a modern white house with floor-to-ceiling glass, clipped hedges in the foreground.

children.text: Rain that arrives sideways
A closed louvered roof stops rain that falls. It does very little about rain that is being driven horizontally, and in the first minutes of a Florida squall a lot of it is.

The practical result: the covered space is dry in the middle and wet for some distance in from whichever faces are open. The dry zone is smaller than the roof, and how much smaller depends on how exposed the lot is and which way the structure faces.

That matters for what you mount underneath. Televisions, speakers, ceiling fans, pendant lights and the cushions that stay outside all belong inside the genuinely dry zone, not merely under the frame. It is also the reason to settle screens during design rather than after: the side channels for a motorized screen mount to the posts, so adding them later means opening finished work. Screens, lighting, fans and the rest of what goes inside the frame are covered in
designing the whole louvered roof system

blog.alt: White louvered roof over an outdoor dining table and chairs beside a two-story stucco house, with ceiling fans mounted under the adjoining covered porch and lawn running up to the patio on both sides.

children.text: What actually fails is the gutter, not the blade
The blades and the seals are rarely the problem. The drainage channels inside the beams are.

They fill with leaf litter, pollen and the fine grit that comes off a shingle roof next to them. The channel backs up, and a backed-up gutter on a closed roof overflows in the only place it can — at the joint between blades. The owner sees water dripping through a closed roof and reports a leak. What it needs is clearing.

How often it needs clearing is set by what is overhead: a live oak or a pine dropping onto the roof is a different regime from an open sky with nothing above it, and a shingle roof next door adds grit that a tile roof does not. It is a hose and a gloved hand rather than a service call, but it is somebody's job, and it should be a question you ask before you buy rather than a discovery you make in year two.
Wind: the rating is two numbers
Ask an installer for the wind rating and you will get a number. Ask which blade position that number is for, and the conversation becomes useful.

Open and closed are structurally different objects. Open, the wind passes between the blades and the frame presents very little surface. Closed, it is a continuous deck that the wind pushes on and — the load that governs almost everything in Florida — lifts. A roof does not get blown down. It gets lifted off.
Most systems therefore carry a higher rating open than closed. The number worth having is
the closed one
, because closed is the position the roof will be sitting in when nobody is home, or when the power went out mid-cycle. A rating quoted without a position is not information you can use.
Where that number becomes about your address

Structures here are engineered to the design wind speed at a specific address, not to "Florida" generally. There are two normal ways to satisfy that — sealed drawings for your site, or a product approval used strictly inside the limits it was tested to — and the review that checks it happens at your county's building department, which is why the process in Alachua is not the process in Broward. That review, and what the two routes mean for your timeline, is covered in
how the permit review works for an open roof structure

The part that carries the load is not the aluminum. It is the anchorage: the size and depth of the footing, the anchor set into it, and the bracket that ties the post to the anchor. Aluminum extrusions from a serious manufacturer are not what gives way. What gives way is a structure fastened to something that was never designed to hold it down.

Two layouts, two versions of that detail. A freestanding roof puts all of the uplift into its own footings, which is why they are larger than people expect. An attached roof hands a share of it to the house at the ledger, and then the only question that matters is what the ledger is fastened into — the structural tie beam, not the fascia board. The wider trade-off between the two layouts is in
attached versus freestanding

blog.alt: White louvered roof over a covered patio on the far side of a pool, with lounge chairs on the deck to the left and a handrail at the pool steps on the right.

children.text: The rule most owners have backwards

A rain sensor closes the blades automatically when it detects rain. For the four o'clock thunderstorm that is exactly right: it saves the cushions and the table while you are at work, and it is one of the better reasons to have the motor at all.

A named storm is a different situation, and for many systems the specified position in sustained high wind is open, so the air moves through instead of loading a closed deck. That is the manufacturer's call for that specific system — it is not a rule we would state for all of them — but here is the part that catches people either way:
an enabled rain sensor will close the blades the moment the rain starts, which is precisely when you least want it making that decision on its own.

So the storm procedure for a motorized roof is never just "open it". It is: put the blades in the specified position, then disable the automation so nothing reverses it, and know how the controller behaves when the power comes back. Ask for that sequence in writing at handover, alongside the remote and the manuals. You will want it at six in the morning with everything else going on, not in a search result.
And when the power is out
Systems differ on what you can do with no power: some have a manual override, some have a battery backup that holds a few cycles, some have neither and the blades stay where they were.

None of those is wrong. Not knowing which one you bought is. It belongs on the comparison list before you choose a system, along with who services it locally and how long parts take — all of which is in
the features worth comparing before you buy
The walk-around after a storm
Not a maintenance schedule. Five things, once the weather clears:
Clear the beam channels and the outlets.
Before the next band, not next weekend. This is the one with the highest chance of mattering.
Run the blades through a full open-and-close cycle and listen.
An actuator that has started to struggle is audible well before it stops, and a part ordered in October arrives faster than the same part ordered in a week when everyone in the county needs one.
Look at the base of each post.
A fresh gap at the anchor plate, a hairline crack radiating out of the footing, a post that is no longer plumb. Any of the three is a call, not a wait-and-see.
Look at where the water came out.
A fan of washed soil or scoured mulch at the discharge point is the site telling you the drainage was sized for less than it got.
Photograph anything that moved, the same day.
A dated photograph is a straightforward insurance conversation. A memory is not.
What this should change about how you buy one
Five things, in writing, before the deposit:

celdas: Why it matters after the first storm
The wind rating with the blade position stated
Closed is the position it will be in when nobody is home
The anchorage detail for your address
Uplift is carried at the footing and the bracket, not by the frame
The discharge point, drawn on the plan
200 gallons an hour has to land somewhere that is not the foundation
The rain sensor's default and the storm instruction can point opposite ways
What the system does with no power
A multi-day outage with the blades stuck shut is the case nobody plans for

children.text: Our estimator prices a motorized louvered roof at $18,000, and that figure is for the structure. Engineered anchorage for a particular site, a real drainage run rather than a splash at the post, and a dedicated circuit for the motor are all site-dependent, and they belong as separate lines on a quote rather than inside a single number —
what moves the cost of a motorized louvered roof
goes through them. If you are still deciding whether a roof that closes is the right structure at all, that comparison is in
pergola versus louvered roof
The short version

A louvered roof handles Florida rain well and Florida wind well, and it does both because of decisions made before the posts went in — where the water leaves, what the posts are anchored to, and whether anyone wrote down what to do when the forecast turns. None of that is visible in a photograph of a finished patio.
That is what a site visit is for: how your lot drains, which faces are exposed, what the panel can carry, and where 200 gallons can actually go. Our
motorized louvered roof systems
page shows how we build them,

faq.answer: It depends on the system, and it is the manufacturer's instruction rather than a general rule. Many systems are specified to be left open in high wind so the air passes between the blades instead of pushing on a closed deck. Get the written procedure for your specific roof at handover, because a rain sensor left enabled will close the blades on its own as soon as the rain starts.
faq.question: Do you open or close a louvered roof before a hurricane?

faq.answer: The middle of it, yes. The edges, no. Rain that arrives sideways comes in under the perimeter on whichever faces are open, so the genuinely dry area is smaller than the roof. Side screens or solid end panels on the exposed faces are what close that gap, and the channels for them mount to the posts during construction.
faq.question: Does a closed louvered roof keep everything underneath dry?

faq.answer: That depends entirely on whether the system has a manual override or a battery backup, and systems differ. It is worth settling before you buy rather than during an outage, because a multi-day outage with the blades stuck closed is the version of this nobody plans for.
faq.question: What happens if the power fails while the blades are closed?

faq.answer: Usually not the blades. It is the drainage: the channels inside the perimeter beams and their outlets fill with leaf litter, the water backs up, and it overflows at the blade seals. To the owner that reads as a roof that leaks, when what it needs is clearing out.
faq.question: What actually fails on a louvered roof in Florida weather?
