children.text: If you already own a pool, the real question is narrower than "new or remodel." It is whether the shell, the location and the layout you have can carry what you want from the backyard. If they can, a complete remodel gets you a pool that looks and runs like new for less than building new, with less disruption. If they cannot, no amount of remodeling fixes a pool that is in the wrong place or structurally finished.
Five questions decide it. Most Florida homeowners who ask us land on a complete remodel.
Question 1: Is the shell sound?

Everything in a remodel rides on the structure. We check the shell and the bond beam for cracks and movement, look at the tile line and the coping for displacement, pressure-test the plumbing, and where there are signs of leaking or settling, look closer at the structure before pricing anything. A sound shell with an ugly surface is the ideal remodel candidate. A shell that has failed is not a remodel; it is a rebuild decision, which we cover separately in
remodel or rebuild
Question 2: Is the pool where you want it?

A remodel cannot move the pool. If the pool blocks the view, sits where the outdoor kitchen should be, or is too close to the house to allow the deck you want, the layout is the problem and new construction is the only route to a different one. If the location works and the complaint is how the pool looks and performs, that is a remodel.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a newly built pool and raised spa, with the deck and fence laid out around fresh lawn.

children.text: Question 3: What do you actually want to change?
Write the list, then sort it into two columns.
Remodel can do this:

interior finish, waterline tile, coping, deck material and extent, equipment (pump, filter, heater, chlorination, automation), lighting, a spa added or rebuilt, a sun shelf cut into the shallow end, steps and benches, water features, a screen enclosure, and a code-compliant barrier.
Only new construction does this:
a different footprint or a substantially larger pool, a different depth profile throughout, a pool in a different place, or a pool and spa designed as one new structure.
If your whole list sits in the first column, the answer is a remodel. Our guide to
what to upgrade during a complete pool remodel
explains how to sequence it so you only open the pool once.
Question 4: How much of the backyard is changing?

A pool is rarely remodeled alone. If you are also adding a pergola, an outdoor kitchen or a screen enclosure, the remodel is the moment to run the gas, electrical and plumbing those need, because the deck is already open. If you are rebuilding the entire backyard around a new layout, that is the case where new construction can make more sense, because the pool is designed with everything else rather than worked around.
Question 5: What does each path cost on your pool?
Prices are specific to the pool, so we do not quote generic ranges. What is consistent is the structure of the comparison:

celdas: Priced from scratch, including rock or water-table work
Resurfaced or replaced; extent can grow
For the scope that counts as construction

what changes the scope of a remodel
and
what moves the price of a new pool
for the levers behind each column.

blog.alt: Remodelled pool and raised spa seen from the corner of the deck, with mature hedge behind.

children.text: The usual answer

When the shell is sound and the location works, a complete remodel is the better decision for most homeowners: the pool you already paid for becomes the pool you want, the work takes weeks rather than months, and the budget goes into finish, equipment and features instead of excavation. New construction is the right call when the shell has failed, when the pool is in the wrong place, or when the whole backyard is being redesigned around a layout the current pool cannot fit.

What a remodel should not be is a surface fix on a pool with underlying problems. Resurfacing a leaking shell or re-tiling over a moving bond beam spends money twice. The difference between a surface job and a complete renovation is the subject of
resurfacing vs full renovation

blog.alt: Newly built pool and raised spa from above, showing the finished stone deck and planting.

We assess the pool you have before we price anything, and we are honest when the answer is "remodel" even though a new build is the larger project. If the pool can carry what you want, see our

cardTitle: New Pool or Remodel the One You Have?

faq.answer: Remodeling the pool you have is almost always less than building new, because the shell, the excavation and much of the deck already exist. Our estimator prices a complete remodel below the same project built new. The exception is a shell that has failed structurally, where the remodel budget is spent on repair before anything you can see.
faq.question: Is it cheaper to remodel a pool or build a new one?

faq.answer: Within limits. A remodel can add a spa, a sun shelf, benches and steps, change the depth profile in places and completely change the finish, tile, coping, deck and equipment. Moving the pool, making it substantially larger, or changing its footprint is new construction.
faq.question: Can a remodel change the shape of my pool?

faq.answer: For most complete remodels, yes: structural work, plumbing, electrical, equipment changes and barrier work are permitted and inspected. Resurfacing-only work is treated differently by different jurisdictions. We confirm the scope with the building department before demolition.
faq.question: Do I need a permit to remodel a pool in Florida?

faq.answer: A condition assessment: visual inspection of the shell and bond beam, a check for movement at the tile line and coping, a pressure test of the plumbing, and where there are signs of leaks or movement, a closer look at the structure. We do this before pricing any remodel.
faq.question: How do I know whether my shell is sound?

children.text: Choose the appliances before the island is designed, not after. In an outdoor kitchen the appliances are not something you drop in at the end — they are the dimensions of the block, the diameter of the gas line, the number of electrical circuits and whether the structure needs a vent hood. Decide them last and you are not choosing appliances; you are choosing whatever happens to fit the holes somebody already built.

That is the whole argument, and it reverses the order most people shop in. What follows are the nine decisions that come before any model number, in the sequence they have to be made. Each one eliminates options, which is the point: by the time you are comparing brands there should be three or four candidates left, not thirty.
What each decision locks into the build

celdas: What it fixes in the construction
Trench route, meter tie-in or tank location
A new trench across a finished deck
Re-running the line, not just the last few feet
Opening the island face, or surface conduit you look at forever
A structural change, not an appliance swap
Block openings and the countertop template

children.text: Read that table as the reason for the order below. Every row is cheap while the kitchen is a drawing and expensive once it is masonry.
1. Natural gas or propane — and is it actually your choice?
The first question is not which grill. It is which fuel, and the answer is usually decided by what already exists at the house rather than by preference.

Natural gas needs a line run from the meter to the island, which is a trench and a tie-in. Propane needs a tank, a location for it that is screened, accessible for exchange or fill, and far enough from the cooking appliances to satisfy the inspector. It also needs someone to notice when it runs out, which is always mid-cook.

Settle this first because it removes half the shortlist immediately. Many appliances are sold for one fuel with a conversion kit available for the other, some are sold for one fuel only, and "convertible" on a spec sheet sometimes means the factory sells a kit rather than that a technician can convert the unit in your backyard. Ask about the specific model, not the brand. The
utilities that have to be run before construction
covers what each choice means for the trench.
2. Size the line for every burner, not just the grill

Homeowners size the gas line for the grill. It has to be sized for everything that can be on at the same time: grill, side burner, power burner, a griddle, a warming drawer, and anything you might add in two years.

The failure here is quiet and permanent. Nothing breaks. The grill simply takes longer to reach temperature, and longer still when somebody is boiling a pot on the side burner. Owners usually blame the grill, and the grill is fine.

Add up the demand for the full set, including the appliance you have not bought yet, and have the line sized for that total. Adding a second cooking appliance later is the moment people discover the line was sized for exactly what was there on day one.
3. Decide the circuits, then check the panel

An outdoor kitchen is rarely one circuit. Refrigeration wants its own, because a shared circuit means the fridge trips on a Friday when someone plugs in a pressure washer and you find out on Sunday. Countertop outlets are another. Lighting, a hood and a television, if there is one, are another again.

blog.alt: Long covered outdoor kitchen against a dark wall: built-in grill, a flat side burner, a stack of stainless drawers and a glass-front beverage refrigerator stocked with bottles, with a television mounted above the counter.

children.text: The constraint people hit is not the island — it is the house panel. If there is no spare capacity, the project includes a sub-panel, and a sub-panel is a cost and a lead time, not a detail to sort out later. Find out early enough that it is a line in the estimate instead of a change order.

Everything in this section has to be in conduit before anything is poured. Retrofitting a circuit into a finished island means either opening its face or running surface conduit down a wall you will be looking at for as long as you own the house.
4. Covered or open — this is really the hood question
Whether to roof the kitchen is a bigger decision than appliances, and it is
its own trade-off in Florida
. But it has to be answered before the appliances, because it decides whether there is a vent hood.

blog.alt: Outdoor kitchen under a palm-thatch roof, with a stainless vent hood over the built-in grill, a ceiling fan hung from the thatch and an undercounter refrigerator at the end of the run.

children.text: A grill under open sky does not need one. A grill under a solid roof or inside a lanai generally does, and the hood is sized to the grill's width and heat output. It needs clearance above it and a duct path to the outside, and both of those are framing decisions. A hood chosen after the roof is built is a hood that turns out to be too small, mounted too high, or ducted through the only beam that could not be cut.
If the ceiling above the grill is wood, the clearance is not a preference. It is a dimension the inspector measures.
5. Which second cooking appliance earns its counter space
Three usually go on the wish list. The number that matters is how many get used.

The honest version of this decision starts with a count: in the last twelve months, how many times did you cook outdoors, and what did you cook? A pizza oven is a Saturday appliance and a genuinely good one for people who entertain. A side burner is a Tuesday appliance. A kamado is a different cooking method, not a second grill, and it gets used by people who already own one.

blog.alt: Poolside outdoor kitchen with a wood-fired oven and its chimney flue standing next to a built-in grill and a side burner, and a sink with a cutting board on the island in front.

children.text: Each appliance you add takes counter length you will want for landing space — the flat run beside the grill where the tray goes down. Outdoor kitchens are far more often ruined by having nowhere to put a hot sheet pan than by lacking a burner.
Laying the kitchen out around the way you actually cook
is where that gets resolved; the decision to make here is simply which appliances get to compete for the space.
6. Cold storage: one appliance, or three
Refrigerator, beverage center, ice maker, kegerator. They are four different decisions that people make as one.

Two things separate them. First, an outdoor-rated refrigerator is a different appliance from an indoor one: sealed against humidity and specified to hold temperature in heat an indoor unit never sees. An indoor undercounter unit installed outside runs continuously, fails early, and the warranty will not cover it — that is not a technicality, it is the first thing the manufacturer asks about.

Second, the ice maker is the one that changes the plumbing. It needs a water supply and it needs a drain, and the drain has to go somewhere that was decided before the slab. Wanting ice after the concrete is poured is an expensive want.
7. A sink, or no sink, and where its drain goes
A sink is the appliance decision that becomes a permit question.

The supply side is straightforward. The drain is the part that varies by county: whether a residential outdoor kitchen sink can discharge to a dry well or has to be tied into the sanitary line is a question your county's plumbing reviewer answers, and the answer is not the same everywhere in Florida. Ask your contractor what your county requires. If the answer is vague, the right time to find out is before the slab, not when an inspector is standing on it.

Worth saying plainly: a lot of outdoor kitchens are better without one. If the back door is fifteen feet away and nobody is washing dishes outside, a sink is a drain, a trench and a permit line in exchange for a place to rinse hands.
8. Build to the spec sheet, not to the category
This is the decision that ruins islands, and it is the least glamorous one here.

A "30-inch grill" is a category. The cutout is a number on that specific model's spec sheet, and it is rarely exactly 30 inches. Different manufacturers in the same nominal size need different openings, different depths and different clearances to combustible material underneath. Masons build to the drawing they were given, so the appliances have to be selected, and their spec sheets in the builder's hands, before block goes up.

The same applies to everything with a door. Which way does it swing, does it clear the walkway when open, is the drawer stack on the side you actually stand on, and does the access door in front of the gas valve leave enough room to reach the valve. These are five-minute conversations at the drawing stage and demolition afterwards.

One more thing belongs here: lead time. An appliance on a long backorder stops being an appliance decision and becomes a schedule decision. Confirm availability at selection, order early, or choose from what can actually arrive before the countertop template is cut.
9. Corrosion — which stainless, and how far you are from salt air
Stainless steel is not one material, and outdoor kitchens are where the difference shows.

The grades usually quoted for outdoor appliances and cabinetry are written as 304 and 430. The cheaper one gives up first at the welds and the fasteners, which is where salt collects and where the protective layer is thinnest, and it is what most bargain door-and-drawer sets are made from. Near salt water that is not a cosmetic issue: it decides how soon the hardware starts staining and how soon it stops closing properly.

Ask for the grade in writing, and ask for it twice: once for the appliances and once for the access doors, drawers and hardware, because they are frequently not the same and the doors are where the saving is made. A rough field check is that the cheaper grade is magnetic and the better one usually is not — useful for catching the obvious case, useless as a certificate.

Then read the warranty. Some manufacturers limit or shorten coverage for installations near salt water, and that is a thing to know before you buy rather than after something pits. Which materials hold up around the appliances — the counter, the facing, the cabinet boxes — is
a separate question with its own answers
Why the order matters as much as the list

Taken in this sequence, each decision narrows the next one. Fuel eliminates appliances. The appliance set sizes the gas line. The appliance set and the roof decide the hood. Cold and water decide the trenching. All of it decides the cutouts, and the cutouts decide the masonry.

Taken in the reverse order — which is how it usually happens, starting with a grill somebody liked at a showroom — each decision contradicts one already built, and the fix is always demolition of something that was finished correctly to the wrong information.
What this means for the budget

Our estimator prices a custom outdoor kitchen at $25,000, and what it shows is a range of plus or minus 10 percent. That number is the kitchen as a built project — structure, counter, utilities and a standard appliance set — not the appliance package priced on its own.

Appliances are the part of that figure that moves the most, because the spread between a competent grill and a top-tier one is wider than the spread in the masonry around it. Beyond the built project, there is no standard number for a particular appliance set, an ice maker's plumbing run or a sub-panel: those come from a site visit.
What actually drives an outdoor kitchen's price
goes through the rest of it, and the
outdoor living cost estimator
will put a range on your version.
If you are still deciding how much kitchen you need at all,
a grill island and a full kitchen are different projects
and the answer changes most of the nine decisions above.
What to bring to the design meeting
Five things, and with them a design meeting produces a drawing instead of a wish list:
Which fuel is available at the house, and where the meter or tank would go.
How many times you cooked outdoors last year, and what you cooked.
Whether the kitchen will be covered.
Whether you want ice, a sink, or neither.
The spec sheets for any appliance you already know you want.
That is what we work from on a
custom outdoor kitchen
, and it is why the appliance conversation happens at the drawing stage rather than at the end. Finished kitchens in
our project gallery
show how the appliance set changes the shape of the island, and
a project estimate
starts with the site visit rather than a number.

faq.answer: Before. Cutout dimensions, gas demand, the number of electrical circuits and whether a vent hood is needed are all built into the island. Selecting appliances afterwards means choosing from whatever fits the openings that already exist.
faq.question: Should I choose outdoor kitchen appliances before or after the island is built?

faq.answer: Sometimes, and not always in the field. "Convertible" on a spec sheet often means the manufacturer sells a conversion kit for that model, which is not the same as a technician being able to convert the unit after installation. Confirm it for the specific model before you buy, not for the brand.
faq.question: Can I convert an outdoor grill from natural gas to propane later?

faq.answer: It depends on what is above it. A grill under open sky does not need one. A grill under a solid roof or a covered lanai generally does, and the hood has to be sized to the grill's width and heat output, with clearance above it and a duct path out. That is a structural decision, not an accessory.
faq.question: Do I need a vent hood over an outdoor grill?

faq.answer: No. An outdoor-rated unit is built differently: sealed against humidity and specified to hold temperature in high ambient heat. An indoor unit put outside runs constantly, fails early, and the manufacturer's warranty will not cover a failure caused by installing it outside its rated environment.
faq.question: Can I use a regular undercounter refrigerator outdoors?

faq.answer: Ask for the grade in writing, separately for the appliances and for the access doors and drawers, because they are often not the same. As a rough field check the cheaper grade is magnetic and the better one usually is not. That catches the obvious case but it is not a substitute for the spec sheet.
faq.question: How do I know which grade of stainless steel I am getting?

children.text: Lay an outdoor kitchen out in this order: find where a drain can fall, find where the smoke goes, draw the path people take from the door to the table, and mark where the afternoon sun lands. The shape — straight run, L, U, or a run with a separate island — is what is left over once those four are settled. Most layout advice runs that sequence backwards, starting from a shape and a work triangle, which is why so many finished kitchens photograph well and work badly in August.
This guide assumes you already know whether you are building an island or a full kitchen. If that is still open, settle it first:
a grill island compared with a full outdoor kitchen
is a different decision, and the two are laid out from opposite starting points. An island gets
placed
. A kitchen gets
routed
The four site facts that choose the shape for you
Before anybody draws a cabinet run, four things about your yard have already eliminated most of the options.

celdas: Where waste can fall to a legal discharge point
Every sink position gravity cannot reach, which often removes one whole side of the yard
Which way the breeze crosses the cooking position
Any arrangement that carries smoke into the seats, the screens or an open slider
The route from the kitchen door to the table
Layouts where the cook, the guests and the food all share one lane
Where the sun is at the hour you actually use the space
West-facing counters, and any seat that is unusable until after dinner

children.text: The drain is the one that moves projects. A supply line can be run almost anywhere; waste has to fall toward something that will take it, and that constraint regularly decides which wing the sink lands in and how far the whole run sits from the house.
Gas, electric and plumbing before construction
covers what each connection needs; for layout, the only thing you need out of it is the answer to "can the sink go there" before you fall in love with a drawing.

The breeze is the one people discover afterwards. Smoke is not a nuisance you get used to — it decides where your guests will and will not sit, permanently. Stand in the yard at the hour you usually cook and watch which way it moves.
The work triangle does not survive the trip outside

The kitchen work triangle assumes a refrigerator, a sink and a range in one room, one cook, and everything else within arm's reach in cabinets. Outdoors, almost none of that holds. Cold storage is a fraction of the volume and the real refrigerator is still in the house. The pantry is in the house. The space usually holds a group and only one of them is cooking. And most of the traffic crossing the area has nothing to do with the meal.
What works instead is simpler. Draw
one line, one direction

: raw food comes in, gets prepped, gets cooked, gets plated, and leaves toward the table. Lay the run so that line travels from one end to the other without doubling back. Then draw the second line — door, drinks, seats — and cross the two as few times as you can.

A layout is failing when the cook has to turn around holding something hot, when plates get set down where raw food was, or when reaching for a drink means standing in the only piece of clear counter. None of those show up in a rendering. All three show up the first weekend.
Landing space is the first thing cut and the only thing missed
Three pieces of counter have a job in every layout, whatever the shape:
Dirty landing.
Where raw food is set down and prep happens, next to the sink if there is one.
Hot landing.
Immediately beside the heat, on both sides of it if two people ever cook together. Everything that comes off a grill has to land within one step.
Clean landing.
Plating and serving, at the end of the line nearest the table.

Here is what happens instead. The appliance list gets fixed early, because appliances are chosen from a showroom and counter is not. Then the run turns out longer than the budget or the wall allows, and the counter shrinks — because it is the only thing on the drawing without a model number attached.
That is the wrong end to trim. An empty cabinet is the cheapest foot of outdoor kitchen you will ever buy; the price sits in the cut-outs, which is the subject of
what actually drives an outdoor kitchen's price

. So when a run has to get shorter, take out an appliance and keep the counter. You use counter every time you cook anything. You use the second side burner roughly as often as you imagined you would.

blog.alt: Long single-wall outdoor kitchen run against a dark textured wall: side burner, built-in grill, drawers, glass-front beverage refrigerator and a wall-mounted television above the counter.

children.text: Which way the cook faces
This costs nothing to change on paper and cannot be changed at all afterwards, which makes it the highest-leverage line in the whole layout.

Facing the house or a back wall gives you the shorter utility runs, somewhere to mount a hood, a screen or storage, and a surface that takes the heat and the splatter. It also puts the cook's back to the pool, the yard and the conversation for the entire evening.

Facing outward fixes that. The cook is part of the party, watches the water, and sees people arrive. The cost is that the run now backs onto something that has to be finished on both sides, and the connections travel further from the building.

In a lot of Florida yards this is settled by one fact that rarely makes it into the design meeting: when the pool is in use, the person cooking is usually also the person keeping an eye on it. If that describes your house, orientation is decided and the rest of the layout works around it.

blog.alt: Outdoor kitchen under a thatched chickee roof with slatted wood cabinet fronts, a dark countertop wrapping into a bar, a stainless hood over the grill and a sink at the far left.

children.text: Bar seating changes a layout more than any appliance
The moment you seat people at the counter, you have put an audience in front of the cook, and two questions follow.

The first is whether the counter steps up. A raised bar hides the working surface from the seats and gives the guests their own ledge, but it blocks the cook's sight line and takes depth off the working side. A single level keeps the conversation open and leaves more usable counter, at the price of everyone seeing the mess. Neither is better; they suit different households.

The second is where the seats go, and there are two hard rules. Not downwind of the grill, and not across the lane between the house and the table. A bar that seats four while everybody edges past it seats two in practice, and the ones at the end learn to stand.
Four shapes, and what each one asks of your site
Once the constraints are on the drawing, the shape is close to decided. This is what each one demands, and where each one runs out.

celdas: What the site has to give you
A wall long enough for the appliances plus landing on both sides of the heat
No corner for prep; landing gets squeezed out as the appliance list grows
A corner and two usable wings
The inside corner is dead counter unless something is designed into it
Three sides and room to stand inside
One cook. A second person is trapped, and the width of the opening governs everything
Depth, and utilities trenched to two places
Two structures, two sets of connections, and the gap between them becomes the traffic lane

children.text: The U renders beautifully and is the one most people point at. The L with the seating on the short wing is the one that tends to survive a crowd and two cooks. If your yard gives you a corner, start there before you commit to wrapping three sides.

blog.alt: L-shaped outdoor kitchen on a travertine deck with black granite counters and a waterfall end, a dark roof post beside the grill run, and a lake and palms behind.

children.text: The posts are part of the layout

If the kitchen is going under a pergola, a louvered roof or a screen enclosure, that structure has footings, and the footings land where the span requires them — not where your counter would like them.

Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500, a motorized louvered roof at $18,000 and a screen enclosure at $15,000, against $25,000 for a custom outdoor kitchen. For layout purposes the numbers matter less than the geometry: post spacing, beam direction and where water comes off the roof are fixed by the cover, and a post landing mid-run — or exactly where two bar seats were drawn — is the most common collision between two otherwise competent designs.
Both drawings need to exist at the same time, before the concrete crew leaves the site. Which cover you build is a separate question, and it changes the post grid:
a pergola compared with a louvered roof
sets out that choice. What cannot wait is the coordination, because the footings go in first and they do not move.
A solid roof adds one more layout consequence: heat and smoke need a path out, and how that is handled can shift where the grill sits within the run. That decision is part of
the nine decisions that come before you choose appliances
The clearances that quietly take counter away
Four of them reorganize more layouts than any aesthetic choice:
The grill lid.
It has to open fully under whatever is above it. A hood, a beam or a low overhang can make a position unusable without anyone noticing until the lid hits.
Combustible clearance.

Every built-in appliance's spec sheet sets a distance to combustible material, and that governs how close the run can sit to a wood post, a screened frame or a cabinet side. Build to the spec sheet, not to the category.
Doors and drawers versus corners.
A refrigerator door that swings into the only walking lane, or a drawer that cannot clear a corner return, is a layout error that looks fine in plan view.
The lane behind the cook.
Whatever you think is enough, it has to work while the cook is bent into a low drawer and somebody is passing with a tray.
Test the layout at full size before anyone lays block
This is the cheapest hour in the project and almost nobody spends it.
Chalk or tape the footprint on the existing slab at full size, including counter depth and any bar overhang.
Put a folding table at roughly counter height where the grill will go, and boxes where the refrigerator and sink cabinet land.
Cook one real meal from it, with the people who will usually be out there.
Write down every time somebody had to move, reach past someone, or walk the long way round.

What that hour reveals, and a drawing never does: the lane behind the cook is too tight once a chair is pulled out; the seats look straight into the smoke; the refrigerator door opens into the walking route; and the counter you designed for plating is the counter everybody puts their drink on.
What locks, and when
Layout freedom disappears in a fixed order, and knowing the order tells you what still deserves argument.
Utilities and trench
— locked at backfill. Moving a sink afterwards means opening the deck.
Cover footings
— locked with the concrete. The post positions are then permanent.
Cabinet geometry
— locked when the block goes up. After that, changes are demolition.
Countertop
— locked at template, which is when the overhang and the seating depth become real.
Appliances
— the last thing you can physically swap, and the first thing that has to be specified, because the cabinets are built to their cut-outs.

Finishes stay flexible longest, but they are not free of layout either: exposure varies across a single run, and which face gets the sun and the rain is worth knowing before you choose. That is the subject of
which materials survive Florida heat, humidity and rain
The short version
Bring these answers to the design meeting and the drawing gets quicker:
Where can waste actually go, and does that rule out a side of the yard?
Which way does the smoke blow at the hour you cook?
Where is the line from the door to the table, and does the kitchen sit across it?
Which way does the cook face, and why?
Is anyone seated at the counter, and does the counter step up?
Where do the cover posts land relative to the run?
Have you stood in the taped footprint and cooked one meal from it?
If you want to see how the sequence runs on a real job — site review, utilities, deck, cabinetry, appliances, inspection — that is the
custom outdoor kitchens
page. Finished layouts of all four shapes are in the
project gallery
, and a
quote from a site visit
starts with the constraints rather than with a shape.

faq.answer: There is no single best shape. The drain route, the direction the smoke travels, the path people take from the house to the table and the afternoon sun rule out most positions before anyone draws a shape. Settle those four and you are usually left with one or two workable arrangements.
faq.question: What is the best outdoor kitchen layout?

faq.answer: It depends on what the cook needs to see. Facing the house keeps the utility runs short and gives you a wall for a hood, storage and a screen, but it puts the cook's back to the pool and the conversation. Facing out solves that and moves the connections further from the building. Decide it on paper, because after the masonry it is not a change, it is a rebuild.
faq.question: Should the grill face the house or the yard?

faq.answer: Enough to set down everything that comes off the heat without taking a step, on both sides if two people ever cook at once. Rather than working from a rule, tape the footprint out at full size and cook one meal from a folding table on the spot. Whatever you found yourself carrying across the yard is the counter that is missing.
faq.question: How much counter space do I need next to the grill?

faq.answer: It works when the seats are out of the smoke and off the route between the house and the table. It fails when they block the lane, because a bar that seats four while people squeeze past it effectively seats two. Where the seats land also decides whether the counter steps up to hide the working surface or stays at one level.
faq.question: Is bar seating a good idea at an outdoor kitchen?

faq.answer: Cheaply, only until the utilities are backfilled and the block goes up. After the trench is closed, moving a sink or a grill means opening the deck; after the cabinets are built, it means demolition. Appliances and finishes stay flexible far longer than the geometry underneath them does.
faq.question: Can the layout still change once construction has started?

children.text: A Florida backyard gets used when it is designed for the climate first. That means shade where people actually sit, protection from afternoon rain and insects, materials that shrug off sun, humidity and salt, and utilities run before anything is built on top of them. Everything else, the furniture, the fire feature, the finishes, is decoration on that frame. This guide is the order we design in, and the reasons behind it.
Design for the climate, then for the look
Four facts drive every decision:
Sun.
Direct afternoon sun makes an unshaded Florida patio unusable for much of the year. Shade is not an accessory; it is what makes the space a room.
Rain.
Summer afternoons bring short, heavy rain. A covered area that stays dry keeps a dinner going; an uncovered one ends it.
Insects.
Screening is the difference between an evening outside and an evening indoors looking at the patio.
Wind.
Structures, screens and roofs are engineered to the wind design for your location under the Florida Building Code. A structure that is not is both a permit problem and a hazard.
Humidity and salt air decide the materials, which we cover below.
The order to build in
Backyards built out of order get dug up. The sequence that avoids it:
Drainage and grading.
Where water goes when it rains, before anything sits on the ground.
Utilities.

Gas to the kitchen and the pool heater, electrical to the equipment pad, the kitchen and the lighting, water and drain to the kitchen sink, conduit for automation and screens. Sleeves under future decks and walkways even for phases you have not committed to.
The pool.
It is the largest excavation and the structure everything else is placed around.
Structures.
Pergola, louvered roof, patio cover or screen enclosure, with footings placed off the pool plumbing.
The kitchen.
On its utilities, under cover.
Decking, finishes, lighting, landscape.
Last, because they are what the earlier work would damage.
Our guide to
utilities an outdoor kitchen needs before construction
is step 2 in detail.

blog.alt: Dark aluminium pergola over a paved pool deck, with palms and water beyond.

children.text: Shade: pergola, louvered roof or cover
The three shade structures solve different problems, and many backyards use two.

celdas: Filtered shade, structure to hang lights and fans, defines the room
Dining and lounge areas that want sky; the pool edge
Shade you can open, and a closed roof in rain
The area where you will eat and sit through a storm
Solid patio cover or lanai roof
Full shade and rain protection, a ceiling for fans and lights
The transition from the house to the pool

children.text: The deciding questions are what you do under it and whether rain matters there.
Pergola vs. louvered roof
walks through the choice;
aluminum vs. wood pergolas
explains why aluminum is the usual answer in this climate.
Screens: rooms, enclosures and motorized screens

Insect protection changes how much the space is used more than any finish does. The options are a fixed screen room or patio enclosure, a pool screen enclosure over the pool and deck, or motorized retractable screens that close a pergola or lanai on demand and disappear otherwise. A pool enclosure can also serve as the barrier that Florida's pool safety law requires. Our pages on
patio screen rooms
pool screen enclosures
and
motorized retractable screens
explain each.

blog.alt: Furnished lanai behind retractable screens, with a sofa, armchairs and a dining table overlooking the pool.

children.text: The outdoor kitchen

An outdoor kitchen is a room, not an appliance. It needs cover, counter space on both sides of the grill, a sink if you will actually cook rather than only grill, lighting over the work surface, and a layout that lets the cook see the pool and the table. The material decisions are about humidity and salt: masonry or framed islands with weather-rated cladding, marine-grade stainless hardware, and appliances built for outdoor use. We cover the choices in
best outdoor kitchen materials for Florida
and the layout in
the outdoor kitchen layout guide
Materials that survive here

celdas: Travertine or pavers on a compacted base; concrete finished for traction
Thin coatings over bad base; untreated wood at the water's edge
Aluminum engineered for the local wind design, powder-coated
Timber without rated hardware and footings
Masonry or framed islands, weather-rated cladding, outdoor-rated appliances, 316 or marine-grade stainless near salt
Indoor appliances, uncovered cabinetry, cheap stainless
Aluminum framing and screen mesh rated for the exposure
Mesh and frames sized for a milder climate
Finishes chosen with the sanitizer in mind; marine-grade metals
Metals that corrode in salt water or salt air
Powder-coated aluminum, teak, solution-dyed acrylic fabrics
Untreated wood, fabrics that fade and hold water

children.text: Lighting and controls

Design lighting in layers: the pool and spa lit as a composition, task light over the kitchen, ambient light under the pergola or roof, and path light where people walk. Put all of it on one control with the pool equipment, so the backyard turns on with one tap. The conduit for every circuit goes in during step 2 above.

blog.alt: Outdoor kitchen with stainless appliances and a stone pizza oven, built under cover beside a pool.

children.text: Landscape that does not fight the pool

Plant away from the water's edge with species that do not drop into the pool, keep root systems away from the shell and the plumbing, and use irrigation that does not spray the deck or the screens. Privacy comes from layered planting and screens rather than a wall of one species. The rule is simple: anything that drops, sheds or seeks water goes elsewhere.
Bringing it together

The backyards that work are designed as one project even when they are built in phases: the pool, the structures, the kitchen and the screens placed together so that footings miss plumbing, shade lands where people sit, and the utilities for phase three go in during phase one. If you want to see your own backyard planned that way, start with a project evaluation on our
custom pool construction
page, or with the
outdoor kitchen
and
aluminum pergola
pages if the pool already exists.

cardTitle: Outdoor Living Design Guide for Florida

faq.answer: Drainage and utilities, then the pool, then the structures, then the kitchen, then the finishes and the furniture. Anything built out of that order gets dug up or worked around later. If the budget is phased, the sleeves, conduit and footings for later phases still go in during the first one.
faq.question: What should I build first in a Florida backyard?

faq.answer: They solve different problems. A pergola gives filtered shade and structure; a motorized louvered roof adds rain protection you can open and close; a screen room or enclosure adds insect protection and can serve as the pool barrier. Many Florida backyards use two of the three together.
faq.question: Pergola, louvered roof or screen room: which one for Florida?

faq.answer: Aluminum structures engineered for the local wind design, travertine or pavers on a proper base, marine-grade stainless and masonry for kitchens, screen rated for the exposure, and pool finishes chosen for the water chemistry. Untreated wood at the water's edge, indoor-grade appliances and uncovered cabinetry are the common failures.
faq.question: What materials hold up outdoors in Florida?

faq.answer: Structures, gas, electrical and plumbing generally do; the building department for your address decides the specifics. Our pergola permit guide covers structures, and gas and electrical for an outdoor kitchen are permitted as those trades.
faq.question: Do outdoor kitchens and pergolas need permits in Florida?

seo.description: How to design a Florida backyard that gets used: sun, rain, insects and wind, the order to build in, materials that last, and how pool, shade and kitchen fit.
seo.title: Outdoor Living Design Guide for Florida Homes

summary: A Florida backyard gets used when it is designed for the climate first: shade where people sit, protection from rain and insects, materials that shrug off sun and salt, and utilities run before anything is built on top of them. This guide is the order we design in.
title: Outdoor Living Design Guide for Florida Homes
titlePage: Outdoor Living Design Guide for Florida Homes

children.text: A pergola beside a pool is not a pergola that happens to be near water. Most of the decisions below change
because
there is water there, and four of them stop being cheap the day the deck is poured.

That is the entire argument for planning the two together. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 whether it goes up with the pool or five years after it. The pergola is not where the money moves. The deck is.
If you take two things from this: decide where the posts land before the deck is poured, and choose the deck material knowing whether a pergola is coming.
The window you are actually working in
Most people arrive at this decision in one of three states, and the state decides how much of the list is still open.

celdas: Post positions, footings, conduit, drainage, bonding
Post positions — pavers lift and reset
Deck poured in concrete or mortar-set stone
Post positions, unless you saw-cut and patch

children.text: None of those is a bad place to be. The third one just costs more to change your mind in, and most people do not know they have walked into it until the pergola contractor is standing on the deck with a tape.
Four decisions that close when the deck does
1. Where the posts land
A pergola post is not held down by its own weight. In Florida it is engineered against uplift, which means a footing sized for the structure — not an anchor bolt into a thin deck slab.

Beside a pool, that footing has to miss three buried things: the pool's bond beam and shell, the plumbing runs between the skimmer, the returns and the equipment pad, and the conduit feeding the light niche. Where those run is known precisely on exactly one day — the day they go in. After that it is memory, a drawing if someone kept one, and a locator.
That is the practical case for one plan instead of two. The information you need to place a footing safely exists at the start and decays afterwards.

There is a comfort dimension too. Measure the walkway from the water's edge, not from the house wall. A post set tight to the coping turns the busiest side of the deck into a corridor, and nobody notices on a drawing.

blog.alt: Dark-framed pergola on a pool deck, with overhead utility lines crossing the sky and a faded wooden gate in the back fence.

children.text: 2. Which side of the pool, and how far back
The Florida problem is the four o'clock sun, not the noon sun.

At noon, shade lands under the structure, which is where everyone assumes it always lands. By late afternoon the sun is low in the west and that shade has moved well to the east of the posts. A pergola placed for the noon photo leaves the seating in full sun at the hour the yard is actually used, which is why the structure usually sits west or southwest of where people sit, set back far enough to block low sun rather than high sun.

Two more things only matter because there is water there. A pool throws reflected light upward, so a structure hard against the coping catches glare and heat under its roof. And a pergola on the wrong axis becomes the permanent view from whichever room faces the yard — worth checking from inside the house before it is staked.
Whether it attaches to the house or stands on its own changes the shade pattern, the drainage and the structure, and that is a decision of its own:
attached versus freestanding
3. The conduit, and the bonding conversation
Everything that makes a pergola worth sitting under is electrical: a fan, lights, a screen motor, speakers, sometimes a TV.

Before the pour, those are sleeves. After it, they are a surface conduit running up a post, or a trench cut across a finished deck. The difference is not subtle and it is decided months before anyone buys a fan.

The part specific to pools is bonding. Aluminum conducts, and metal near pool water belongs to the pool's equipotential bonding grid — a conductor installed under the deck, before it is closed. Adding a metal structure afterwards means either proving the bond already reaches it or creating one, which is an electrician's job and a far easier one while the grid is still exposed. Get the electrician and the pergola installer to agree, in writing, on who ties it in and at what stage. Left implicit, each assumes the other has it.
Pool lighting is priced in our estimator at $450 per fixture. Lighting a pergola is a different system with no line in that table, which is a reason to have it quoted rather than assumed.

blog.alt: Dark bronze aluminum pergola with pale translucent roof panels beside a pool and spa, with a black electrical cable left hanging from the frame where a light fixture will go.

children.text: 4. Where the rain goes

An open slat roof lets rain through and nothing changes. A solid panel or a louvered roof does not, and that is the point of it — but it also takes everything that used to fall across the whole roof and delivers it in a line at one edge.

Three things follow. The roof should not drain toward the pool, or every storm puts roof water and whatever was on the roof into the water you are balancing. Many aluminum systems drain internally through the posts, which is tidy and requires knowing where the post is going before the deck slope is set. And the discharge point has to exist somewhere — a deck poured to drain away from the pool does not automatically have a place for a concentrated flow.
Pool decks are poured with slope in them. That slope is set once.
Four that stay open, and still change the design
5. Roof type: open slats, solid, or louvered
The usual framing is rain protection. Beside a pool there is a better question: do you want the water shaded?

Shaded water is colder water. A pool covered for most of the day in January is a pool that leans on its heater — priced in our estimator at $4,500 — far more often than the neighbor's. Which is why the answer, in most Florida yards, is to shade the people and leave the water in the sun.

That points to a structure set beside the pool rather than over it, and it changes what the roof has to do. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a louvered roof at $18,000; the gap is the mechanism and what it buys you is choosing, storm by storm, between sun and cover. Whether that is worth it in your yard is the whole of
pergola versus louvered roof
, and if you are leaning that way,
motorized louvered roof systems
is the build it becomes.
6. The barrier line

A residential pool needs a barrier, and what forms it varies: a fence, a screen enclosure, the house wall with alarmed openings, or some combination. It is drawn on a plan and confirmed at an inspection.

A structure built beside the pool can touch that line. Posts landing next to a fence, a bench or a low wall within reach of it, a roof a barrier ties into — each of those is something a reviewer looks at, not a matter of opinion. The fix is procedural: ask the pergola contractor to show the barrier line on their own drawing, and submit the two together where the county allows it. If the pergola sits inside the barrier, it is a non-issue. If the barrier has to pass around it, that is a thing to design rather than discover.
How the submittal itself works, and what it depends on, is in
do you need a permit for a pergola in Florida

blog.alt: Aluminum patio cover next to a pool, with a removable mesh safety fence, sheets of construction plastic on the grass and a ribbed downspout at the corner of the house.

children.text: 7. What lives underneath, and what the water does to it
The first several feet out from the coping get wet, and not with rainwater. It is treated pool water, arriving as splash and as whatever comes off people walking out.
That zone is where post bases, furniture, rugs, cabinetry and a television end up if the pergola sits close to the pool. Powder-coated aluminum handles it differently from wood, which is most of
how aluminum and wood compare over a Florida decade
. The floor is your deck, priced in our estimator at $12 per square foot in concrete, $22 in pavers and $35 in travertine.
If an
outdoor kitchen
is going under there — $25,000 in the estimator — it brings gas, water and a drain across the same ground as the pool's plumbing, which puts it back in the first section of this list.
8. What the structure has to carry later
A pergola is a frame, and frames get things hung on them for years afterwards.
A ceiling fan needs a beam and a box designed for it, not a bracket added later.
Motorized screens
need track space inside the beam and power at the head. Specified now, it is a detail; retrofitted, it is a different frame.
Heaters, speakers and a projector each want a mounting point and a circuit.
Sizing a structure for something you might add costs very little at the drawing stage. It is the only item on this list that is cheap to over-plan.
What the wrong order actually costs

The pergola line does not move. Our estimator prices it at $8,500 whenever it goes up. The cost of doing it in the wrong order lands entirely on the deck, and how hard it lands was decided by the surface.

Pavers lift, the footing goes in, the pavers reset. There is labor and some breakage, and a seam where the reset batch has weathered differently from the rest. Poured concrete and mortar-set travertine do not lift. They are saw-cut, broken out, footed, and patched — and the patch is visible for as long as the deck exists.

One way to read that: at $12 per square foot for concrete and $22 for pavers, a 600-square-foot deck in pavers costs about $6,000 more. If a pergola, an enclosure or a kitchen is even a possibility later, part of that $6,000 is buying the option to change your mind without cutting the deck open. If the yard is genuinely finished on day one, it is not.
The same logic runs through the rest of the build in
the upgrades worth planning before construction
, which is the pool-side view of this same overlap.
One submittal or two

Our estimator prices permits at 9% of the pool plus the deck. The pergola is not in that base — as a separate structure it generally carries its own review, including the wind and anchoring side, and which department sees it in what order depends on the county rather than on Florida.

What is worth knowing is the shape of it. Two projects a year apart are two submittals, two review cycles and two sets of inspections on overlapping ground. One project is one set of drawings that already shows where the posts, the bonding and the barrier are. Ask who submits, and when.
Turning this into a number
The figures above are the ones behind the site's
pool cost estimator

, and what it returns is a band of roughly ±10% rather than a price, because two identical structures in two different yards are not the same job. What moves the pergola side of that band specifically is in
what changes a pergola's price
; what moves the pool side is in
what a custom pool really costs
Put both into the same number before the meeting. A pergola added to a budget that was fixed around a pool is the classic way an $8,500 line turns into a conversation about cutting the deck.
If you want to see how the two get built as one scope, that is on our
aluminum pergola construction
and
custom pool and spa
pages, there are finished yards in the

faq.answer: Yes. What changes is the footing. A post carries uplift as well as weight, so it needs a footing sized by the engineer rather than an anchor into a thin deck slab. On a paver deck the pavers lift, the footing goes in and the pavers reset. On poured concrete or mortar-set stone it means saw-cutting and patching.
faq.question: Can I add a pergola to a pool deck that is already finished?

faq.answer: Usually the seating. Shaded water is colder water, and a pool that gets no winter sun leans on its heater far more often. The structure normally goes on the west or southwest side of where people sit, set back far enough that late-afternoon sun is blocked rather than noon sun.
faq.question: Should the pergola shade the pool or the seating area?

faq.answer: A metal structure close to pool water is part of the bonding picture, and the equipotential bonding grid is installed under the deck before it is poured. Ask the electrician and the pergola installer to agree in writing on who ties it in and at what stage, rather than assuming the other one has it.
faq.question: Does an aluminum pergola beside a pool need to be bonded?

faq.answer: It is a separate structure, so it usually carries its own review, including the wind and anchoring side of it. Which department reviews it and in what order depends on the county. The useful question to ask the contractor is who submits it, and whether it goes in with the pool drawings or after them.

children.text: Six of the seven decisions below are locked the day the posts go into concrete. The one about what runs inside the frame is locked earlier than that, when the frame is fabricated. That short window is the whole problem with a pergola: it is a small project next to a pool or a kitchen, it gets decided quickly, and most of the regret afterwards comes from decisions nobody knew they were making.
Take them in the order below. Each one narrows the next, and running them out of order is how a pergola ends up the right size in the wrong place.
When each decision closes

celdas: Saw-cutting, a new footing, a patched slab
Nothing structural, but the shade stays wrong
Re-engineering the frame and the footings
Footings and what they sit in
Surface conduit on a finished frame
Paying for the same footings twice

children.text: Two decisions that are not on this list
Two questions come up first in almost every pergola conversation, and both are large enough to deserve their own answer rather than a paragraph here.
What it is made of.
Aluminum and wood age very differently in Florida humidity, and the comparison is in
aluminum versus wood pergolas over a Florida decade
Whether it touches the house.
Attached and freestanding are different structures with different post counts and different permitting, and that choice is worked through in
attached versus freestanding pergola layouts
Settle both before you start on the seven below. Everything here assumes they are already answered.
1. How big, measured from the furniture rather than the slab
The size of a pergola is not a design preference. It is the output of a furniture plan.

Decide what actually happens under it — a dining table, two loungers, a bar, a grill — and lay it out on the ground with tape before anyone draws a structure around it. Then walk it. Pull a chair back from the table the way people really do and see where your heel lands.
Two things about the numbers on a pergola drawing are worth knowing before you read one:
The outside dimension is not the usable area.

Posts sit inboard of the beam line, and the beams overhang the posts. A structure described as twelve by twenty has a smaller clear span between its posts, and that clear span is what your furniture has to fit inside. Ask for it separately.
The shaded area is smaller than both, and it moves.
A roof throws shade at an angle that changes through the afternoon. At the hours you actually use the space, part of the footprint is in sun. Which hours those are is decision three.

The structure should also be smaller than the paving under it, not the same size. A slab sized exactly to the pergola puts chair legs off the edge, and that is a mistake you notice every time somebody sits down.

blog.alt: Timber pavilion with a gable roof and exposed trusses bolted with steel plates, covering an outdoor kitchen with two built-in grills, a stone island with bar stools and ceiling fans hung along the ridge.

children.text: 2. Where the posts land

A post is the only part of a pergola that is genuinely in your way, and post positions are usually set by the structure rather than by you. That is fine, as long as you check them against how the space is used before the footings are poured.
Five places a post causes a problem, in rough order of how often it happens:
In the walking line between the house door and the pool or the grill.
Inside the swing of a slider or a French door.
At the edge of a pool deck, where it narrows the walkway to a squeeze. If a pool is part of this project,
the features worth planning with a poolside pergola
covers the rest of that overlap.
Centered on a window, so the view from inside the house now has a column in it permanently.
Where the mower and the irrigation have to get past, which is how posts end up with a permanent ring of dead grass around them.
Moving a post on a drawing costs nothing. Moving it after the footing is poured means breaking out concrete, pouring a new footing, and living with a patch in the paving.
The view from inside the house is the one people check last and regret most. Stand at the kitchen sink and the living room sofa, look out, and have somebody hold a broom where each post is going.
3. Which way the shade falls, at the hours you use it
A pergola does not shade a space. It shades part of a space, at particular hours, depending on which way its roof members run.
So the decision starts with a question about your week rather than about the structure:
when will you actually be out there?
Lunch on a Saturday and six o'clock on a Tuesday are different problems, and a roof optimized for one is mediocre at the other.
Three things follow from the answer:
Roof density.

Widely spaced slats read as an open frame and shade very little at midday. Tighter spacing shades more and darkens the space under it. If the hours you named are the hot middle of the day, you are probably looking for more density than the drawing shows.
Which way the slats run.
Fixed slats block sun from one direction better than the other. Running them the wrong way relative to the sun at your hours produces stripes when you wanted shade.
What no roof can fix.
Late afternoon sun comes in low and sideways, under any roof at any density. A west-facing patio at six o'clock is not a roof problem. It is a side problem, solved with planting, a privacy panel, or
motorized retractable screens
— and if screens are even a possibility, that has consequences in decision seven.

The cheapest way to check any of this is to stand on the spot at the hour in question, a week before the drawing is approved. Photographs of finished structures are useful for a different purpose — our
project gallery
shows how the same roof density reads on different houses — but they cannot tell you where your own sun is at five.
4. What the roof does when it rains
There are three families of pergola roof, and the choice between them is not really about how they look. It is about where the water goes.

celdas: Nothing underneath can mind getting wet
Gutter, downspout, and a discharge point
The same, plus a heavier frame and bigger footings

children.text: An open slat roof is a sun structure, not a rain structure. That is a perfectly good thing to build, as long as you know it: a dining table under open slats is fine, and an outdoor kitchen under open slats is an outdoor kitchen in the rain. If appliances are going under this structure, see
what an outdoor kitchen needs from the space around it
before you settle the roof.
The moment the roof sheds water, a second decision appears that most homeowners never get asked about:
where the downspout discharges.

Concentrating a roof's worth of rain next to the house foundation, onto a pool deck, or at the top of a slope toward a neighbor is a worse problem than the one the roof solved. It needs a run of pipe to somewhere that can take it, and that pipe is buried — which means it happens before the paving, not after.

A solid roof also changes the structure itself. It catches wind in a way an open frame does not, which affects the frame, the footings, and what gets reviewed when the drawings are submitted. What that review involves where you live is in
whether a pergola needs a permit in Florida

blog.alt: Attached patio cover with translucent roof panels over a red brick paver patio, with two blue planters and a pair of metal chairs in front of the French doors of a tile-roofed stucco house.

children.text: 5. What it stands on
A patio slab is not a foundation. It is a surface.

Pergola posts have to resist uplift, which is the load that matters for a roof in Florida, and that resistance comes from footings under the posts rather than from the slab around them. On an existing patio, the normal sequence is to saw-cut the slab at each post, dig, pour the footing, and patch. The patch is visible unless the paving can be re-laid over it.
Which gives a simple piece of sequencing that saves real money:
If new paving is part of this project,
the footings go in before the paving is laid, and the patch never exists.
If a pool deck is being poured,
the pergola footings and any sleeves for water, gas or power go in at the same time. The same logic governs the rest of that deck — see
what to plan before a pool deck is poured
If the paving is staying,
budget the cut and the patch openly rather than discovering it as a change order.

How deep and how wide the footings are is an engineering answer for your specific site and structure, not a rule of thumb, and it is one of the things a submitted drawing exists to show. A contractor who can tell you what the footings are and why is a contractor whose drawings have been through that review before.
6. What runs inside the frame
Fans, lights, a heater, speakers, an outlet, a screen motor: every one of them is wire, and on an aluminum pergola the wire runs inside the posts and beams.

That makes it a fabrication decision, not a shopping decision. The frame is cut, drilled and assembled with those runs in it. Adding them afterwards means surface conduit stuck to a finished structure, which is exactly as good as it sounds.
Two details that get missed even when the wiring is planned:
A fan needs structure, not just power.
A fan hangs off a beam and moves while it does it. The beam that carries a fan is specified differently from the beam that holds a light, and that specification happens before anything is cut.
Circuits, not just outlets.
Lights, a couple of fans, a heater and a television are not one circuit. What the panel can give this structure is worth knowing before the trench is dug, because the trench is the expensive part.
The split is the same one that governs pool equipment: you can defer the purchase, you cannot defer the buried half. Buy the fan next year if you want. Put the conduit and the blocking in this year.

blog.alt: Freestanding dark aluminum pergola with translucent roof panels beside a pool, with a slatted privacy panel under it and two thin black cables left hanging from the frame.

children.text: 7. What you are leaving room for
The last decision is about the version of this backyard that exists in three years.
Provisions are cheap while the frame is being made and expensive afterwards. The ones worth asking about:
A column profile and header depth that will accept a
screen track
, whether or not screens are being bought now.
A
gas, water or drain stub
to the corner where a grill or a kitchen would go.
Conduit toward the house
for a controller, a television, or lighting you have not chosen yet.
Enough
footing and frame capacity
for a heavier roof, if the roof might change.

That last one is where the money is. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a louvered roof at $18,000 as line items on a backyard project, and the arithmetic looks like it favors starting small. It usually does not, because replacing one structure with the other means paying twice for footings, permitting and installation, and the second set is more expensive than the first — it happens inside a finished yard. If a louvered roof is what you actually want, the comparison to make now rather than later is in
pergola versus louvered roof

Those estimator figures are starting configurations, not quotes, and the estimator shows every total as a range of plus or minus ten percent for exactly that reason. What moves a pergola away from its starting figure — span, roof type, footings, finish — is broken down in
what changes an aluminum pergola's price
. You can run your own combination through the
backyard project estimator
The order, one more time
Settle material and attachment first; they are separate questions.
Lay out the furniture. The footprint comes from it.
Place the posts against doors, walkways, sightlines and the mower.
Name the hours you will use the space, then choose orientation and roof density.
Decide whether the roof sheds water. If it does, decide where the water goes.
Put the footings in before the paving.
Put the wire and the blocking in before the frame is cut, and leave the provisions for later in while it is cheap.

Every one of those seven is permanent once the structure is up. None of them are expensive to get right at the drawing stage, and all of them are expensive to correct afterwards — which is the only real argument for spending an afternoon on a roll of tape and a broom handle before anything is ordered.
How we work through this sequence, and what ends up on the drawing before anything is fabricated, is on the
custom aluminum pergola builders
page. A
project estimate
starts with a site visit, because decisions two through five cannot be made from a floor plan.

faq.answer: The furniture layout. Size and post positions both come out of it, and both are permanent once the footings are poured. Tape the furniture plan onto the slab and stand in it before anyone draws a structure around it.
faq.question: What should I decide first when planning a pergola?

faq.answer: Usually, but the slab is not the foundation. Posts carry uplift and need footings under them, which normally means saw-cutting the slab, digging and pouring, then patching. If you are laying new paving anyway, the footings go in first and the patch never exists.
faq.question: Can a pergola be built on my existing patio slab?

faq.answer: You have to choose whether they are coming. The wiring runs inside the posts and beams, and the beam that carries a fan is not the same beam that holds a light. The fixture itself can be bought later; the conduit and the structure to hang it from cannot be added later without opening the frame.
faq.question: Do I have to choose fans and lights before the pergola is built?

faq.answer: Only if its roof sheds water rather than letting it through. An open slat roof does not. A solid or translucent roof does, and that turns into a second decision most people skip: where the downspout discharges. Next to the house foundation or onto a pool deck is worse than the problem it solved.
faq.question: Does a pergola need gutters?

faq.answer: Only if the upgrade is genuinely years away. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500 and a louvered roof at $18,000, but replacing one with the other later also means paying for footings, permitting and installation a second time. If the louvered roof is the real goal, the cheaper path is usually building it once.
faq.question: Should I build a pergola now and upgrade to a louvered roof later?
