children.text: Of the ten upgrades on a typical pool proposal, four close permanently the day the shell is poured, three stay inexpensive forever as long as something goes into the ground on the right day, and three you can still change your mind about after the excavator has left. Nobody sorts the list that way for you, so it gets treated as one decision about money. It is really three decisions about timing.

A pool is built in a fixed sequence: excavation, steel, plumbing rough-in, shell, tile and coping, deck and electrical, interior finish, startup. Every upgrade has a stage after which adding it stops being an addition and becomes a demolition. That stage, not the price, is what should decide the order you settle things in. The sequence itself, and what tends to move it, is in
the Florida pool construction timeline
The rule behind all ten
An upgrade is expensive later only if something has to be buried for it to work.

Water lines, electrical conduit and structure all go in before the concrete. Anything that bolts onto a finished pool — a cleaner, a cover, furniture, most of what sits on the equipment pad — costs roughly the same in year five as in year one. Run every line of your proposal through that single question and the list sorts itself.
When each upgrade closes

celdas: Last stage it can be added cheaply
Cutting and rebuilding a finished shell
The same — it is shell geometry
Opening the shell and the deck
A niche cut into cured concrete
Rough-in for tees and electrical capacity
Conduit from the pad to the house
Sleeves for a kitchen, pergola or enclosure
Any time, if the materials suit it
Demolition, a second pour, a second permit

children.text: The four that close with the shell
1. The spa

A spa shares steel and concrete with the pool and is poured on the same day. Our estimator prices an integrated spa at $12,000 and a spillover spa at $18,000 — both of them as part of the original build, because that is the only form in which either one is an upgrade rather than a rebuild.
Whether a spa belongs in your project at all is a separate question, worked through on
the list of decisions to settle before excavation
. What belongs here is only the deadline, so that it does not make the decision for you: the window is steel, not tile.
2. Sun shelf, bench and entry steps
These are not fittings installed in a pool. They are the shape of the hole, formed in steel and poured with the walls.

Three things worth settling while they are still drawings: how deep the sun shelf is and how many chairs genuinely fit on it; whether the bench is at the end you will sit at or the end you will swim to; and whether the entry is a corner set of steps or a full-width one.

Depth is where the sun shelf goes wrong, and it goes wrong in both directions. Deep enough to feel like part of the pool is too deep for a lounger to stand level in it; shallow enough to hold the chairs properly is shallow enough that nobody swims over it. Decide which of the two the shelf is for while it is a drawing, because afterwards it is the shape of the concrete. The entry has the same either-or: a full-width set of steps looks generous and eats swimming length, and a corner entry keeps it.

blog.alt: Two white loungers standing in the shallow sun shelf at one end of a rectangular pool, with a raised spa faced in blue mosaic at the far corner and a lake and palms beyond the deck.

children.text: 3. Water features
Bubblers, deck jets and spillovers are plumbing. Each one is a line run before the shell goes up and a valve or a dedicated pump back at the equipment pad.

The detail most people find out too late is that they want them on separate valves. A spillover runs constantly and becomes background; bubblers are charming for an hour and loud for an evening. Separately valved, you choose. Shared off one line, you get all of them or none of them, and correcting that afterwards is a dig.

blog.alt: Raised spa faced in dark blue mosaic under white coping, spilling over its edge into the rectangular pool below, with submerged entry steps and a clipped hedge behind a black metal fence.

children.text: 4. Light niches, and how many

Our estimator prices pool LEDs at $450 per fixture, so the difference between one fixture and three is $900 — decided before the shell goes up, because a niche is formed into the wall rather than drilled into it afterwards.
The count follows the shape, not the square footage. A fixture throws in one direction, so a pool with a deep end, a spa and a sun shelf has three areas that each go dark on their own.

Which wall each niche goes in matters as much as how many there are, and it is the part that never reaches the proposal. A fixture set in the far wall throws its light away from the house and the seating; the same fixture in the near wall throws it back at the people looking at the water. Ask which wall, not just how many. Lighting the house and the yard is a separate system — see
permanent soffit and LED lighting
— but the path it travels runs under your new deck, which is item 7.
The three that only need something in the ground
5. Heating

Our estimator prices a heater at $4,500. You do not have to buy it with the pool. You do have to leave it somewhere to go: space on the equipment pad, plumbing tees in the right place, and electrical capacity at the panel.
The equipment is a purchase and can wait. The tees and the capacity are construction and cannot. Split them on the proposal and deferring the heater costs you nothing except the heater.
6. Automation
Our estimator prices automation at $3,500. It is the upgrade most often deferred and most often regretted, because deferring the controller is fine and deferring the conduit is not.

What has to happen at rough-in is small: a conduit run from the equipment pad to wherever a panel or an indoor control will live, and equipment selected now that will accept a controller later. Neither of those is the $3,500. Both of them are the reason the $3,500 is still $3,500 in three years. Our guide to
pool automation for new construction
lists everything that has to be buried.
7. Sleeves, footings and whatever comes next

Everything else you will ever build in that yard has to cross ground the pool crew is already standing in. Our estimator prices a pergola at $8,500, a louvered roof at $18,000, a screen enclosure at $15,000 and an outdoor kitchen at $25,000 — and all four need something underneath before they can exist.
An
outdoor kitchen
needs gas, water, drain and power reaching it.
A
pergola
needs footings where its posts land, which means knowing now where the posts land.
A
screen enclosure
anchors into the deck, so the deck has to be built to carry it.
Landscape lighting and irrigation both need a route under the deck rather than across it.
None of that commits you to building any of them. It commits you to knowing where they would go. Where each one should sit is a planning question, handled in
the pre-excavation list
; what belongs in the trench on the day it is open is this one.
The three still open after the shell
8. Salt chlorination
Our estimator prices salt chlorination at $2,200, and it carries almost no timing penalty: the cell installs at the pad, on equipment that is already there.

Salt or chlorine is a question about how the water feels and how you handle it day to day, and it belongs with the pre-excavation decisions rather than with these ten. The part that belongs here is the one with a deadline, and it is the material one. Coping, deck surface and any metal close to the water are specified during design, and specifying them for a salt pool costs nothing at that point. Add the cell in year one or year five — but if the materials were chosen for a different pool, that is what you are converting into.
9. Deck size and material
The deck is poured late, which makes it feel like a late decision. It is not one: the size goes on the permit application, so it is fixed months before anybody pours it.

Our estimator prices decking at $12 per square foot for concrete, $22 for pavers and $35 for travertine. On a 600-square-foot deck that is $7,200, $13,200 and $21,000 — a spread of $13,800 on the item most likely to be skimmed at the end of a long meeting. Size matters as much as surface, because permitting is calculated on the whole: our estimator prices permits at 9% of the pool plus the deck. Enlarging a deck afterwards is demolition, a second pour and a second permit on top.
A raised or structural deck is a different build again — that is
custom deck construction
, not paving around a pool.
10. Interior finish

Our estimator applies a multiplier to the shell: plaster counts as one, pebble as 1.15, a premium finish as 1.35. On a 450-square-foot standard pool at the estimator's $85 per square foot, the shell is $38,250 — so pebble adds about $5,700 and a premium finish about $13,400. The permit line follows it, because the estimator charges permitting as a percentage of the pool after the multiplier, not before it.

It goes in after everything else, which makes it the last upgrade you can still change your mind about, and the one that does most to the color of the water. It also has the shortest window at the other end: once it is applied, changing it means draining and resurfacing the pool.

blog.alt: Rectangular pool with a pale blue interior and a step edged in dark tile, beside a raised spa clad in dark blue mosaic and a pale stone deck running out to a strip of lawn.

children.text: Why there is no price for adding it afterwards
There is no price list for adding things to a finished pool, because it is not a separate job. It is the same job plus undoing whatever is in the way, and the cost is dominated by the undoing.

One part of it can be priced, though. Our estimator prices renovation at 82% of what the same result would cost as new construction — an 18% discount for a shell, a deck and a permit that already exist. That is the clearest thing the estimator says about how little credit you get for what is already standing.
That is the arithmetic behind the split running through this whole list. Deferring a purchase costs you the purchase. Deferring the burial costs you the pour.
Two lines worth asking for in the proposal
Every upgrade as its own line, accepted or declined, including the rough-ins.
A sleeve that is a favor is a sleeve that does not get laid on a busy morning. A sleeve that is a line item gets laid.
The stage each upgrade closes at, written beside its price.
Any builder running the sequence knows it without looking. In writing, it turns "we can look at that later" into a date.
How changes get priced and approved once work has started is a different conversation, and it is in
the ten questions to ask before you sign
. The stage list is what tells you when you have stopped having a choice at all.
Working the upgrades into the number
The figures above are the ones behind the site's
pool cost estimator

, and what it returns is a band of roughly ±10% rather than a price, because two identical pools in two different yards are not the same job. The eight decisions that move the base number before any upgrade is added are in
what a custom pool really costs in Florida
Add the upgrades into that band before the meeting rather than after it. Pool budgets rarely fail on one expensive item. They fail on four reasonable ones agreed after the number was already fixed.
When the list is ready to become a scope,
our custom pool and spa construction
page sets out how the build is staged, and a
project estimate
starts with a site visit rather than a number.

faq.answer: Four of them are part of the shell rather than additions to it: a spa, the sun shelf and bench and step geometry, the plumbing for water features, and the light niches. All four are set in steel and buried in concrete, so adding them afterwards means cutting into a finished pool.
faq.question: Which pool upgrades are impossible to add later?

faq.answer: The heater, the automation controller and salt chlorination, provided the construction handles the buried half: plumbing tees and electrical capacity for the heater, conduit from the pad to the house for the controller, and materials around the water specified for salt. Deferring the purchase costs the purchase. Deferring what gets buried costs the pour.
faq.question: Which pool upgrades can I defer without paying for it twice?

faq.answer: Yes, provided the construction left room for it: space on the equipment pad, plumbing tees in the right place, and electrical capacity at the panel. Our estimator prices a heater at $4,500 and salt chlorination at $2,200, and neither number changes much later. What changes is whether the buried work has to be redone first.
faq.question: Can I add a heater or a salt system after the pool is finished?

faq.answer: Anything that would otherwise have to cross it later: gas, water, drain and power sleeves toward a future outdoor kitchen, conduit for landscape or soffit lighting and for irrigation, and the footing locations for a pergola. If a screen enclosure is likely, the deck also has to be built to carry its anchors.
faq.question: What should go under a pool deck before it is poured?

faq.answer: It is the one upgrade on this list that stays open almost to the end, because the finish is applied after the shell, tile and deck are done. Our estimator applies a multiplier to the shell: plaster counts as one, pebble as 1.15 and a premium finish as 1.35. Once it is applied, changing it means draining and resurfacing.
faq.question: Does the pool interior finish have to be chosen early?

children.text: A louvered roof is bought, not built. The frame arrives cut to your opening, engineered by whoever manufactures it and approved as a configuration rather than as a one-off design. The installer anchors it, powers it, drains it and stands behind it. That changes which questions are worth your hour: most of what decides whether you are happy in year six comes down to which system was quoted and what happens after the truck leaves, not to how the crew behaves during the week they are there.

Our estimator prices a motorized louvered roof at $18,000 before site conditions, which is enough money to be worth asking properly. The general contractor questions — license, change orders, payment schedule, references — still apply, and they are already covered in
the ten questions to ask any builder before you sign
. Do not spend your hour re-asking those. Ask these instead.
If you only ask three
Which system are you quoting, by name, and are you the dealer for it?
What configuration is it approved for at my span and post spacing — can I see that page?
Who services it in year six, and which parts are proprietary?

The first tells you what you are actually buying. The second tells you whether the plan will clear review at the size you were shown. The third tells you what year six feels like, which is the question nobody asks and everybody eventually lives in.
1. Which system, by name?

A quote that says "motorized louvered pergola, 16 x 20, powder-coated aluminum" describes a category, not a product. Two of those quotes are not comparable, and the cheaper one is cheaper for a reason you cannot see.
Ask for the manufacturer and the model line in writing. Then ask a second question that sounds redundant and is not:
are you the dealer for this system, or are you buying it through someone else?

Both arrangements can work. But they behave differently the day something breaks, because the manufacturer's warranty is normally administered through its dealer network, and if your installer is not in it, your claim goes through a company you never met.
Follow it with: how many of this exact system have you installed, and when was the last one? Installers move between product lines. Someone fluent in one brand's bracketry is learning on yours.
The feature-level comparison between systems — blade profile, span, motor type, seals, controls — is a separate exercise, and it is in
the seven features worth comparing before you buy
. Do that comparison first if you have not; this conversation goes better when you already know what you are looking at.
2. What is it approved for at my size?
This is the question that separates people who have permitted these before from people who have not.

The engineering does not belong to the brand. It belongs to a configuration: a blade length, a beam span, a post spacing, an attachment method, a wind zone. The same system that is approved at one span may not be at the next one up. So "it's rated for Florida" is not an answer, and neither is a wind speed quoted from memory.
What to ask for: the approval the system will be permitted under, and the page of it that covers
your

span and post spacing. An installer who works with the product routinely can pull that up. One who cannot is going to discover the limit during plan review, and you will find out as a redesign — usually an extra post landing in the middle of the space the roof was built to open up.
Two follow-ups worth the breath:
Which approval does my county accept?
That varies, and the answer should be a document, not a reassurance.
Is the attachment part of the approval, or is it being engineered separately?
Attaching to an existing house is where a manufactured system stops being manufactured, and it is where a separate engineer's sign-off often has to appear.
While you are here: ask who pulls the permit. The answer should be the contractor, under their own license.

blog.alt: White louvered roof attached to the back of a two-story white house, covering a gray tile terrace with a low white daybed and a dining table, with a tall hedge at left, a neighbor's barrel tile roof beyond it and lawn in the foreground.

children.text: 3. Where does the water actually go?

With the blades closed, a louvered roof is a roof. The perimeter beams are the gutter and at least one post is the downspout, so every drop that lands on it leaves the structure at one point, at grade, in a yard that used to receive that rain spread across its whole footprint.
The question is not "does it drain." It is:
which post, onto what, and running where from there?
Ask to see the discharge point marked on the drawing. Then ask three things about it:
Does it tie into an existing drain, or does it daylight onto the yard?
Where does that water go once it is on the ground — toward the house slab, the neighbor's side yard, or somewhere that genuinely drains?
What happens in a real Florida downpour rather than an average one?

This is the item most often left for the crew to solve on installation day, and it is how a new roof creates a wet corner that was not there before. It is also the cheapest thing in the entire project to get right on paper and one of the more expensive to fix afterward.

One more, specific to here: leaves. The blade seals and the beam channels have to stay clear, and under oaks that is not optional. Ask what the cleaning access looks like on the system being quoted — whether it is a hose from the ground or a ladder and a removed end cap.

blog.alt: White louvered roof on slim posts over a pale tile patio still wet from rain, with a white perimeter fence, a canal and palms behind it and solar panels on a neighbor's roof.

children.text: 4. Who does the electrical, and is it in this number?
The motor needs power. So does the controller, and so will the lights, fans or heaters that get added under the frame later — which is most of them.
How the whole system gets designed together
covers what belongs inside the frame; here the question is narrower and it is about scope.
Ask plainly:
is the electrical in this quote, and who holds the license for it?
Then:
Dedicated circuit, or tapped from an existing exterior outlet?
Is that work permitted and inspected on its own, and is that in the price?
If the panel is on the far side of the house, what does getting power to this corner involve — and is that trenching line-itemed or assumed?

The last one moves real money and is the single most common thing missing from a low quote. A quote that includes the structure and leaves the circuit to you is not a cheaper quote; it is an incomplete one.

While the beams are still open, settle the conduit for whatever comes later. The frames are hollow. Wiring runs inside them if it was planned and on the surface if it was not, and that difference is visible for as long as the structure stands.

blog.alt: Louvered roof with a dark bronze frame and white blades over a concrete courtyard, in front of a modern white house with floor-to-ceiling glass, a black safety fence and a clipped hedge in the foreground.

children.text: 5. If it attaches to the house, what is it attaching to?

A freestanding unit stands on its own footings and sidesteps this entirely — at the cost of larger footings and posts that take up floor space. If yours attaches, this is the question that decides whether you have a leak in year three.

Ask what is behind the surface it lands on. Fascia board over truss tails, a block wall, a concrete tie beam and a stucco band each carry load differently, and they are not interchangeable. Then ask how the connection is flashed and sealed, and — the part people skip —
who owns that joint if it ever weeps.
The manufacturer warrants the frame. The connection to your house is the installer's work.

If the person quoting cannot tell you what is behind that fascia, they have not looked yet, and the ledger detail is being decided on the day by whoever is holding the drill. The trade-offs between the two layouts, including what each does to footings and drainage, are in
how attached and freestanding structures compare
6. What does each warranty cover, and who honors it?

"Fully warrantied" covers nothing you can rely on later. There are four or five separate warranties stacked on a louvered roof, with different lengths and different owners. Ask for them as separate lines.

celdas: How long, and does it transfer if you sell the house?
What voids it — salt exposure, pressure washing, certain cleaners?
Component maker, usually the shortest term
Is the labor to replace a failed part included, or only the part?
How long, and what happens to it if the company closes?
Which of the two above is that?

children.text: The gap that catches people is the third row. A part warranty on a motor sounds generous until a failure inside the term means a free actuator and a paid service call to fit it. Ask which it is, in writing, before the money moves.
7. Who services it in year six?
Everything above is answerable on a good day. This one is about a bad one.
Who services this system locally — you, or a third party?
Are the controller and actuators proprietary to this brand, or standard parts?
What is the parts lead time, and does that change if the system is imported?
If I call four years from now because one blade is not rotating, what is the process, and is there a trip charge?
Those four answers predict how you will feel about this roof far better than any spec sheet. A failed actuator is a two-week inconvenience or a two-month one depending entirely on them.

Ask for one more thing at handover: the model and serial numbers and the parts list, on the closeout paperwork. It costs the installer nothing on the day and it is what lets a different company help you if the original one is gone.
How the system behaves in Florida rain and wind
covers what it is being asked to survive between service calls.
8. What is my deposit actually buying?
This is the question no contractor-hiring article covers, because it only exists when the thing you are buying is manufactured.
At some point the order releases and the extrusions get cut to your opening. After that date, a size change is not a change order — it is a new order. So ask:
What date does the order release?
What confirms the final dimensions before then: a field measurement, or the drawing?
What portion of the deposit is non-refundable once it releases?
What is the lead time in weeks?
What happens if the permit comes back with comments after the order has released?

That last one is the reason the second question in this article matters so much. An order released against a configuration that review will not accept is how a project acquires both a delay and a restocking problem at the same time.
9. What does the yard look like the day the crew leaves?

Footings in an existing paver deck mean cores cut through finished paving. Ask who supplies the replacement pavers and whether they will match — a dye lot from four years ago usually does not. In a concrete slab, ask who patches and accept now that the patch will be visible.

Also ask where the equipment stages, what happens to the irrigation heads in the work path, and who restores the grass. None of these are deal-breakers. All of them are cheaper to agree on before they happen.
10. Can I see one you installed four or more years ago?
Every one of these looks identical when it is new. Year four is where the finish, the seals, the drainage and the service record become visible.

Ask for an older reference rather than a recent one, and near salt if your project is. Then ask that homeowner a single question: when you called about something after the final payment, what happened?
What the quote should say
Before you compare two of these on price, check that both say all of this in writing:
Manufacturer and model line
Exact dimensions, post count and post locations
The approval the configuration is permitted under
Where the water discharges, and where it goes from there
Electrical scope, and who is licensed for it
Each warranty as its own line, with its own term
Lead time in weeks and the order-release date
Who restores the paving or slab around the footings

Two quotes that both contain those eight items are comparable. Two that do not are just two numbers, and the lower one is usually lower because something on this list is missing from it rather than because it is a better deal. What actually moves the total is broken down in
the seven factors behind a louvered roof's price
, and if you are still deciding whether the motor earns its keep at all,
the comparison against a fixed pergola
settles that faster than a feature list.
Where this goes next

With a specific backyard on the table, most of these questions answer themselves during a site walk: where the sun comes from, what the fascia is made of, where the panel is, and where water can go. Our
motorized louvered roof systems
page shows how we build them,
the gallery
has finished ones you can look at, and a
project estimate
starts with that walk-through rather than with a number.

faq.answer: It depends on where it leaks, which is exactly why you separate the warranties before you sign. Water coming through the blades or the beams is a product question. Water coming in where the frame meets the house, or standing where the downspout discharges, is an installation question. Ask both parties' coverage to be written as separate lines on the quote.
faq.question: If the roof leaks, is that the installer or the manufacturer?

faq.answer: The motor and controller need power, and that work is licensed and inspected like any other exterior circuit. What varies is whether it is inside the quote or left for you to arrange afterward. Ask which, and ask whether the circuit is dedicated or tapped from an existing outdoor outlet.
faq.question: Do I need a licensed electrician for a motorized louvered roof?

faq.answer: The lead time is set by the manufacturer's production queue and by whether the system is made domestically or imported, so there is no single number. Ask for it in weeks, in writing, along with the date the order releases — because after that date the extrusions are cut to your dimensions.
faq.question: How long does a louvered roof take to arrive after ordering?

faq.answer: Manufacturer and model, the exact dimensions and post count, the approval the configuration is permitted under, where the water discharges, who does the electrical, each warranty as its own line, the lead time, and who restores the paving or slab around the footings.
faq.question: What should be on the quote besides the price?

children.text: Rebuild your pool for one of two reasons: the shell has stopped doing its structural job, or the pool is in the wrong place. Nothing else on the usual complaint list — dated finish, cracked deck, obsolete equipment, a shape you stopped liking years ago — requires demolishing anything. That is all remodel work, and our estimator prices a remodel at 18% below the same finished project built new: about
less on a project that comes out at roughly
new.
So this is a diagnosis, not a budget exercise. Price the two paths after you know what you have, not before. Below is the order to check in, and the first check that fails is the one that decides.
The five checks, in order
The shell.
Is it still structurally sound?
The position.
Would you put a pool there today?
The geometry.
Can the shape and depth you want come out of the walls you already have?
The buried work.
Plumbing runs, equipment pad, electrical service.
Everything around it.
Deck, coping, barrier, enclosure.
Checks 1 and 2 are pass or fail. A shell that has failed, or a pool sitting in the wrong part of the yard, sends you to a rebuild regardless of what the rest says.
Checks 3, 4 and 5 decide nothing by themselves. They tell you how much of the remodel saving is actually there, which is a different question and the one most quotes get wrong.
Why the price gap is not what decides this

The 18% is a discount on a project the estimator assumes can reuse the shell, the hole and the plumbing already in the ground. That assumption is exactly what check 1 tests. Run the remodel number before anyone has looked at the shell and you have priced a scope you have not confirmed you can buy.

So price is the second question here, not the first. How that discount behaves as the scope grows — what it covers, what it does not, and why it is worth more on a big project than a small one — is worked through in
what actually changes a remodel's scope
. For the broader comparison of the two routes, budget and disruption included, read
new pool construction vs pool remodeling
. This article is only about which of the two your pool needs.
Check 1. Is the shell still doing its job?
This is the only check that can end the conversation on its own, and the only one you cannot do from a deck chair.

What matters is not whether there are cracks — nearly every older concrete pool has some — but which kind. Fine, shallow crazing across the plaster is a surface condition. A crack that runs in a line through the finish and into the shell, that has a lip you can feel with a fingernail, that reappears in the same place after being patched, or that is echoed by a matching crack in the deck above it, is movement. Movement means the shell is working against the ground instead of with it.
Four other findings point the same way:
Rust staining bleeding through from behind the finish
, which means the steel inside the shell is corroding and expanding.
Hollow or drummy areas
where a tapped surface sounds different, which means the finish has separated from the concrete beneath it.
A leak that persists
after skimmer, returns, lights and equipment have all been ruled out.
Visible movement in the structure itself
— a coping line that no longer runs true, a raised wall that has tipped, a bond beam that has separated from the deck.
One or two of these usually means a repair. Several together, or a single structural crack that has moved twice, usually means the shell has reached the end.
Two practical notes. First, none of this can be judged through water and twenty-year-old plaster, so a real answer requires the pool drained. Second,
draining a Florida pool is not a homeowner job.

Groundwater can float an empty shell out of the ground, which is exactly what the hydrostatic relief valve in the floor is there to prevent, and in wet ground that valve is not always enough. The inspection and the draining get planned together, by whoever is going to be standing in the pool.
Check 2. Would you put a pool there today?
Nothing in a remodel moves the pool. Not one foot. If the pool is in the wrong place, a remodel spends real money making a badly located pool nicer to look at.
Stand in the yard and answer honestly:
Is it in sun when you would use it, or in the shadow of the house by three in the afternoon?
Is it far enough from the house that nobody walks out to it, or so close there is no room for seating between the two?
Does the yard drain toward it?
Did the setbacks, the septic field or the easements put it where it is, rather than anyone choosing?
Does an old screen cage decide the shape of everything around it?

blog.alt: Aerial view of a pool and spa on a wide deck beside a single-storey house, with a garden hose running across the deck and a wood ranch fence around the pasture beyond.

children.text: A pool that has to move at all is a rebuild. A pool that is in the right place with the wrong deck around it is a remodel and a deck job — which is usually the cheaper problem, even when the deck is the larger number.
Check 3. Can the shape you want come out of the shell you have?
More can be done inside an existing shell than most people expect, and the dividing line is simple:
do the existing walls stay where they are?

Work that keeps the walls in place is structural remodeling. Filling in a deep diving well to get a usable depth, cutting in a sun shelf, raising a wall to carry a spillway, squaring off a kidney shape at one end, adding an integrated spa against an existing wall — our estimator prices that spa at
, or
with a spillover, whether it goes on a new pool or an old one.

Work that moves the walls outward is a new shell. It can be sold as a remodel, and the deposit will be smaller, but you are paying for excavation, steel, concrete and a full inspection sequence. That is a rebuild of part of the pool, and it should be priced and permitted like one.

There is a middle path worth asking about: rebuilding a section while keeping the rest. It is common where one end of a pool is failing or where a diving well has to go, and it prices between the two. What it is not is a way to avoid the structural question in check 1 — a partial rebuild attached to a failing shell is money spent on both.
Check 4. The plumbing you cannot see
This is where remodel savings quietly evaporate, because the reuse everyone is counting on is buried.

Ask for the suction and return lines to be pressure tested before anyone commits to a scope. Ask how the lines are routed and whether they run under the deck or under the shell. Ask whether the equipment pad can stay where it is, and what the electrical service at the pad will support — a heater at
, a salt system at
and an automation panel at
are all standard remodel line items, and all of them assume power that is already adequate.

blog.alt: Pool with a raised spa and travertine coping, two chaise loungers standing in the shallow end and a covered lanai with patio furniture behind.

children.text: If the answer is that the lines have to be re-run, a good share of the reuse saving goes with them, and the honest comparison changes. That is not a reason to rebuild by itself. It is a reason to know before you sign, rather than at week three.
Check 5. The deck, the barrier and everything around the water
On most remodels the deck is the biggest single number after the pool itself, and people are consistently surprised by it.
Our estimator prices decking at
$12 per square foot
in concrete,
in pavers and
in travertine. On a 600-square-foot deck that is

— a spread as wide as the entire interior finish decision. If the existing deck is cracked, sloped toward the house or the wrong height against a new coping line, it is coming out, and it belongs in the comparison from the start.

blog.alt: Aerial view of a pool behind a house, ringed by removable mesh safety fencing, with a yellow plastic slide, a gas grill and an orange kayak on the lawn.

children.text: Two more items around the water change the arithmetic:
The barrier.

Any work that opens the pool area affects the safety barrier, and it has to be in place and compliant when the job closes. Removable mesh fencing, a compliant gate, or an enclosure all count differently.
The enclosure.
If a screen cage has to come apart to get an excavator into the back yard, that cost belongs to the rebuild path, not to the pool. An enclosure prices at
in our estimator, which is what makes this a decision rather than a detail.
Pool screen enclosures
are worth planning in the same conversation if yours is near the end of its life anyway.
What a rebuild actually costs, which is not the new-construction number
New construction figures — ours included — assume an empty yard. A rebuild starts with an excavator removing a pool that is already there, and then builds the new one.

There is no demolition line in the estimator, because demolition is not estimated from a table. It is driven by three things: how an excavator reaches the back yard, how large and how deeply reinforced the old shell is, and how much deck comes out with it. A pool behind a house with a wide side gate and one behind a house with a narrow gate and a screen cage are not the same job.
So the comparison is not remodel versus new. It is:

celdas: New finish, new equipment, deck work, some structural work — at 18% below the new-build figure
The above, plus excavation, steel and concrete for the section being replaced
Demolition and disposal of the old pool, plus the full new-construction price

children.text: Permits scale with scope on all three paths. The estimator carries permitting and engineering at
9% of the pool and deck

, which means the same review cost that a new build carries arrives with a remodel the moment the structure, the depth or the electrical changes. A finish-only project usually does not trigger that; a structural one usually does. What each county reviews, and in what order, varies — the part that does not vary is that the contractor pulls the permit under their own license and the work gets inspected.
Four findings that look like a rebuild and are not
A rough, stained, patchy interior.
That is the finish, not the shell. It is the most common reason people assume a pool is finished, and it is a resurfacing job —
what resurfacing covers and what a full renovation covers
sets out the difference.
Fine crazing across the plaster.
Shallow, map-like cracking in the finish is normal aging in a plaster surface.
A leak.
Most leaks are fittings, light niches, skimmer throats or the plumbing — all repairable without touching the structure. The shell is the last suspect, not the first.
A shape you have stopped liking.
Much of that is coping, waterline tile, finish color and what is behind the pool rather than the outline itself.
Our gallery
is the fastest way to see how much changes above the waterline.
The option nobody quotes you

If the yard would genuinely be better without the pool, removing it is a real answer. It is not the right answer often — but it is worth five minutes before committing a remodel budget to a pool nobody in the household has swum in for three years.
How to get to an answer in a week
Have the shell inspected properly, drained, by the contractor who would do the work. This is the check that decides, so do it first.
Walk the yard and answer check 2 out loud, before you are attached to a design.
Write down the finished result you want — depth, shape, spa, deck, shade, what runs after dark. Not the work, the outcome.
Run that same outcome through the
pool cost estimator
twice, once as new construction and once as a remodel, and see how much of the gap is the pool and how much is everything around it.
Then get a site visit, and make the contractor tell you which of the five checks their price assumes.

Worked in that order, the decision is usually already settled by check 1 or check 2, and what was left to argue about turns out to be scope. That is the useful outcome: it moves the conversation from what the pool costs to what it needs.
If you want to see how we run that inspection and what a scope looks like when it comes back, that is on the
pool remodeling and renovation
page. If the shell turns out to be finished,
custom pool and spa construction
is the other path, and a
project estimate
starts with the site visit rather than a number.

faq.answer: Age on its own decides nothing. A concrete shell that was built well and has not moved can be resurfaced and re-plumbed repeatedly. What forces a rebuild is a shell that has lost its structure or a pool sitting somewhere you would not put one today.
faq.question: Does an old pool have to be rebuilt?

faq.answer: Our estimator prices a remodel at 18% below the same finished project built new — around $16,600 on a project that prices at about $92,000 new. Because it is a percentage it grows with the size of the project, and it assumes the existing shell can be reused. If the shell cannot be reused, the saving that number is built on is not there.
faq.question: How much cheaper is remodeling than rebuilding?

faq.answer: Sometimes. Filling in a deep diving well, adding a sun shelf or raising a wall for a spillway is structural work done inside a shell that stays where it is. Moving the walls outward is a new shell, which is a rebuild whatever it gets called in the quote.
faq.question: Can the shape or depth of an existing pool be changed?

faq.answer: It is higher. New construction figures assume an empty yard, and a rebuild starts by demolishing and hauling away a pool that is already there. How much higher depends on access to the back yard, the size of the old shell and how much deck comes out with it.
faq.question: Is a rebuild the same price as building a new pool?

faq.answer: Not safely in most of Florida. Groundwater can lift an empty shell out of the ground, which is what the hydrostatic relief valve in the floor exists to prevent. Draining should be planned by the contractor who is going to do the inspection, and usually only when the water table allows it.
faq.question: Can I empty my pool to inspect the shell myself?

children.text: A residential pool and a commercial pool in Florida are built with the same materials by the same kind of crew, and from there the paths split. A residential pool is governed by the Florida Building Code's residential swimming pool chapter and the Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act, permitted and inspected by the local building department, and designed to the owner's taste. A commercial pool is also a public pool under the Florida Department of Health's rule, which adds a second permit, a prescribed set of engineering requirements, and obligations that continue after the pool opens.
This guide lays the two side by side for owners, boards and developers deciding which project they actually have.
Which rules apply

celdas: Florida Building Code, residential swimming pool chapter
Florida Building Code plus Florida Administrative Code Chapter 64E-9 (public pools)
Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act (barrier or equivalent)
Public pool rule: barriers, signage, lifesaving equipment, suction-outlet protection
Federal accessibility standards apply to public accommodations
The rule prescribes hydraulics, treatment, markings, decks, lighting and more

children.text: The classification is not a choice. If the pool serves more than one household, it is almost always public, and the Department of Health makes the determination. Our guide to
commercial pool construction for decision-makers
covers the classification in more detail.

blog.alt: Long lap pool from above, set in a lawn beside a covered lanai and a lake.

children.text: Who permits and inspects

celdas: Department of Health construction permit before building, operating permit before opening
Building department at stages, plus Department of Health before opening and periodically after
Engineer-sealed plans drawn to the public pool rule, reviewed by both agencies

children.text: For the residential side,
which permits a Florida pool needs
walks through the package and the inspection sequence.
What the design has to include

A residential pool is designed around how a family will use it: the shape, the spa, the sun shelf, the finish, the lighting, the features. The code sets the floor, mainly on structure, electrical, suction outlets and the barrier, and the owner chooses everything above it.

A public pool is designed to a rule that specifies the turnover rate and filtration, the disinfection and pH control, the depth profile and markings, deck widths and drainage, lighting, ladders, handrails and lifelines, the equipment room, chemical storage, signage, and an accessible means of entry. Aesthetics are layered on top of that; they do not replace it.

blog.alt: Backyard pool and raised spa seen from the deck, with the house and palms behind.

children.text: Construction and equipment

The shell of a gunite public pool is built the same way as a residential one, engineered for its size and the ground it sits in. The differences are in what is attached to it: larger filtration sized to the required turnover, automated chemical control that most operators need to stay within the rule, flow meters, a dedicated equipment room, deck drainage that returns nothing to the pool, and lifesaving equipment and signage at opening. Suction-outlet protection is required on both, but a public pool's design is reviewed for it explicitly.
Cost and schedule

A public pool of a given size costs more than a residential pool of the same size, and takes longer, because the rule prescribes more, the engineering is heavier, and two agencies review and inspect. We do not publish per-square-foot comparisons because they misrepresent both: on a residential pool the price is set by design choices the owner makes, and on a public pool by the treatment system, the deck program and accessibility more than by the water. A realistic number for either comes from a design, not a formula. For residential pools, our
pool cost estimator
prices the design choices; for commercial projects, we price from a program and an engineered concept.
Operation after opening

A residential pool is the owner's to run. A public pool is operated under the Department's rule, with records, inspections and responsibilities that continue for the life of the pool. The operator should be in the room during design, because equipment choices decide how hard that job is.

blog.alt: Lap pool seen from under the aluminium patio cover, with loungers on the paved deck.

children.text: Licensing

Florida's pool contractor licenses distinguish scope. A contractor licensed for commercial pool work can build residential pools as well; the reverse is not automatic. Before hiring for a community or hotel pool, check the license category on the DBPR site, not only that the number exists. We build both under our state licenses, which are published on every page of this site.
Which project do you have?
If one household will use the pool, it is residential: see our
custom pool construction
page and the
complete guide to pool construction in Florida
. If a community, a property or paying guests will use it, plan it as a public pool from the first meeting: see our
commercial and multifamily services
page, and let us confirm the classification with the Department of Health before the design starts.

cardTitle: Residential vs Commercial Pools in Florida

faq.answer: It depends on the license category. Florida's pool contractor licenses distinguish residential and commercial scope; a contractor licensed for commercial pool work can build both. Check the license category, not just the number, on the DBPR site.
faq.question: Can a residential pool contractor build a commercial pool in Florida?

faq.answer: The public pool rule prescribes filtration, treatment, markings, decks, lighting, accessibility and equipment-room requirements that a residential pool does not need, the engineering is heavier, and two agencies review and inspect the work. The pool itself is a smaller share of the budget.
faq.question: Why does a commercial pool cost more than a residential pool of the same size?

faq.answer: No. A single-family residential pool is governed by the Florida Building Code's residential swimming pool chapter and the Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act, enforced by the local building department. The Department of Health's public pool rule does not apply to it.
faq.question: Does a residential pool have to meet any public pool rules?

faq.answer: A pool serving one single-family rental is generally residential. Pools serving multiple units, a community or paying guests are generally public. When in doubt, ask the Florida Department of Health before design; the classification changes the whole project.
faq.question: Is a pool at a rental property residential or commercial?

children.text: Luxury in a Florida pool is not a feature list. It is a pool that fits the house and the lot, with finish, tile, coping, deck and lighting chosen as one palette, the equipment out of sight, and the details resolved before the shell is shot. The ten directions below are the ones we build most in North and South Florida. For each, we note what it asks of the site and the budget, because a design that ignores either is a mistake with a nice rendering.
1. The geometric pool with a raised spa

A rectangle or a clean L-shape, a raised spa at one end clad in mosaic tile with a spillway into the pool, and a deck that runs the width of the house. It suits contemporary and Mediterranean homes alike, reads as custom from the first photograph, and is forgiving on narrow lots.
What it asks: a spa shares plumbing and heating with the pool, so its position is decided with the hydraulics. The spillway is a detail that has to be built, not added.

blog.alt: Raised square spa clad in pale mosaic tile spilling into a rectangular pool, seen from the pool deck.

children.text: 2. The sun shelf pool

A shallow ledge, usually along one side or across the entry, where loungers sit in a few inches of water. In Florida it is the most used square footage of the pool: children play on it, adults read on it, and it is where bubblers and umbrella sleeves go.
What it asks: the shelf is part of the shell, so it is in the engineered plans. Bubbler plumbing and umbrella sleeves go in before the shell is shot. Our guide to
upgrades worth planning before construction
lists what cannot be added later.
3. The infinity or knife-edge pool
The water appears to run over an edge into the view. It belongs on a lot with a view to fall into: a lake, a golf course, a slope. On a flat suburban lot it is an expensive way to look at a fence.
What it asks: a catch basin, a second pump and careful hydraulics; the edge is a structural element engineered to tight tolerances. Both are decided in design.
4. The pool with integrated lighting design

Underwater LED lighting is standard. Designed lighting is different: lights positioned so the pool, the spa spillway and the water features are lit as a composition, with deck and landscape lighting on the same control, and no fixture pointed at the house.
What it asks: fixture positions and niches in the shell, transformer capacity, and conduit for the deck and landscape circuits, all before the deck is poured. Automation ties it to one app; our
pool automation for new construction
guide explains what to decide.
5. The dark-finish pool

A dark plaster, quartz or pebble finish turns the water a deep blue or green, reflects the sky and the house, and reads as a natural pool or a reflecting pool. It is the single finish choice that changes a pool's character most.
What it asks: dark finishes warm the water faster and show chemistry problems sooner. In Florida that is a trade-off worth understanding before you choose; we cover it in
dark pool finishes in Florida

blog.alt: Two-storey Florida home with a geometric pool, raised spa and white stone deck running the width of the backyard.

children.text: 6. The pool and pergola designed together

A pergola or louvered roof over part of the deck, placed so that shade falls where people sit and the structure frames the pool from the house. When the two are designed together, the footings miss the plumbing, the deck pattern aligns with the posts, and the pergola's electrical runs in the same trench.
What it asks: a single plan. Our guide to
a pergola beside a pool
lists the eight things to settle together.
7. The spa-forward design

For homes where the spa is the point, especially in North Florida where the cooler months are real: a larger spa, a spillway that is the focal point from the lanai, lounge seating with jets planned to the people who will use it, and a heater sized to bring it up quickly.
What it asks: heater capacity and gas or electric supply, planned with the equipment pad. Read
pool and spa or pool only
for the decision itself.
8. The plunge pool or spool
A compact pool, sometimes with spa jets and a heater, for lots that cannot fit a full pool or owners who want to cool off and soak rather than swim. On a courtyard lot it can be the whole backyard.
What it asks: the same engineering as a full pool in a small footprint, which is why it is not cheap per square foot. Luxury here is entirely in the finish and the deck.
9. The pool with water features

Sheer-descent waterfalls from a raised wall, deck jets arcing into the shallow end, bubblers on the shelf, a spillway from the spa. Water in motion masks road noise and makes the pool read as alive from inside the house.
What it asks: every feature is plumbing, a pump or a valve, and often a structure. They are designed in, with the hydraulics sized to run them.
10. The screened resort pool

A pool and deck under a screen enclosure, with the enclosure's roof line following the house and the panels sized so the view reads as open. In Florida it is the most practical luxury: no insects, less debris, lower chemical demand, and it can serve as the code-required barrier.
What it asks: the enclosure is a structure engineered for the local wind design, with its own footings and permit. Its columns are placed with the pool and deck so nothing lands on plumbing. See our
pool screen enclosures
page.

blog.alt: Pool and raised spa seen across the lawn, with palms and the rear of the house behind.

children.text: How to tell a design idea from a design mistake
Three tests, in order:
Does it fit the lot and the house?
Scale, sight lines from the main rooms, setbacks and easements. A 3D model against the real lot answers this before engineering.
Can it be built as one system?
Hydraulics, structure, electrical and the barrier all have to carry it. Features that are "added later" usually cannot be, or cost more than the pool did.
Will you use it in August and in January?
Shade, a heater, a screen and lighting are what make a Florida pool a year-round room rather than a summer photograph.
Our guide to
what makes a pool look custom
covers the nine detail choices that separate the two. When you are ready to see your own lot in 3D, request a project evaluation on our
custom pool construction
page.

cardTitle: 10 Luxury Pool Designs for Florida Homes

faq.answer: Coherence. A luxury pool is sized and shaped to the house and the lot, its finish, tile, coping and deck are chosen as one palette, the equipment is hidden and the lighting is designed. Adding features to a pool that does not fit the space makes it expensive, not luxurious.
faq.question: What makes a pool design luxury rather than just expensive?

faq.answer: The ones you will use most of the year: a sun shelf, a spa for the cooler months, shade over part of the deck, and lighting that makes the pool usable after dark. A heater extends the season in North Florida. Features chosen for a photograph are the ones that go unused.
faq.question: Which luxury pool features are worth it in Florida?

faq.answer: Yes. Several of the designs here, the geometric pool, the plunge or spool, and the courtyard pool, are built for compact lots. Luxury on a small lot comes from proportion and finish, not size.
faq.question: Can a small backyard have a luxury pool?

faq.answer: A dark finish absorbs more sun and the water warms faster and reads a deeper color. In Florida that is welcome in winter and a consideration in summer; shade, water features and a chiller are the usual answers. Our guide to dark pool finishes covers the trade-offs.
faq.question: Does a dark pool finish make the water hotter?

children.text: A pool reads as custom when its geometry agrees with the house behind it. Not when it has more features. Four choices carry most of that read — where the pool sits relative to the house's lines, how much deck surrounds it and on which side, whether anything rises above the waterline, and whether coping, waterline tile and deck were chosen as one decision — and all four are settled on the layout drawing, before anybody prices a finish.

That is the useful part. The choices that do the most cost the least, and the ones that dominate a quote show the least when the geometry underneath them is ordinary. A long feature list on a badly placed pool still looks like a catalog pool.
Here are the nine, roughly in the order they get locked.
The four that do most of the work
Alignment with the house.
Deck proportion — how much, and on which side.
One element above the waterline.
Coping, waterline tile and deck decided together.
Everything after those is refinement.
1. Where the pool sits relative to the house

The common default is to center the pool on the yard. The better default is to align it to something the house already has: the opening of the main slider, a column line on the lanai, the outside face of the rear wall.

There is a quick test for this on the drawing. Lay a straightedge along each jamb of the main slider and run those two lines out into the yard. The pool's near edge should either land on one of them or clear them by a wide, obvious margin. What you do not want is a miss of a foot or two — that is the condition that reads as accidental from inside the house, and it is the one nobody notices on paper.

A pool centered on the lot but aligned to nothing on the house reads as dropped in, and the giveaway is usually a wedge of deck on one side that nobody uses and nobody can explain. A pool that shares a centerline or an edge with the architecture looks designed even when it is a plain rectangle.
This costs nothing to get right on paper, and it is the most expensive item on this list to change once the layout has gone to the county.
The twelve decisions worth settling before excavation
covers what else locks at that same moment.

blog.alt: Two-storey house with a covered lanai and outdoor dining set beside a rectangular pool, a blue-tiled raised spa at the far corner, and grass strips set between paver squares in the foreground.

children.text: 2. Deck proportion — how much, and on which side
Deck is where budgets get trimmed first, and it is the main thing separating a custom-looking pool from a stock one.

The mistake is uniform width: the same three or four feet all the way around. Real use is never uniform. The house side carries furniture and traffic and wants depth. The far side often only needs walking room. One side frequently wants none at all — lawn or planting running straight to the coping is a deliberate move, not a saving.

It is worth pricing that extra depth against the feature it would be traded for, because the comparison usually surprises people. Our estimator prices paver decking at $22 per square foot and travertine at $35. Widening one 30-foot side by three feet is 90 square feet: roughly $2,000 in pavers, $3,150 in travertine. That is less than most water features, and it changes the proportion of the entire yard rather than one corner of it. What deck size and material do to the total is in
the decisions that move a Florida pool's price
3. One element above the waterline

A pool that is entirely flat reads flat, however good the outline is. One vertical element — a raised spa, a raised bond beam with sheet falls, a planter wall at the far end — gives the eye a plane above the water. That plane is the only surface on the whole project that gets seen dry, at eye level and lit after dark, and it gives the pool a back, so the view from the house stops at something instead of running out.

Which element to build is a question about where people sit, not about the feature list. From a seat in the lanai a raised wall lands near eye level and closes off the far end of the water. That is a focal point if you wanted one and a wall if you did not. Walk to the chair you will actually use and look at that height before the wall is drawn.
One is usually enough. Two competing raised elements on a suburban lot start to read as a display rather than a yard.
Whatever you choose is structural: it is formed with the shell and poured once. The prices for each kind are in
what a custom pool really costs

blog.alt: Curved pool with three sheet waterfalls falling from a long raised wall of pale blue mosaic tile, a matching raised spa spilling into the water alongside it, and tall palms and a fairway beyond a black metal fence.

children.text: 4. Coping, waterline tile and deck as one decision
These three materials touch each other, and they are usually chosen at three different times, from three different sample sets, under showroom lighting.

Choose them together, outdoors, at something close to the real size. A warm travertine coping against a cool grey deck looks fine on a sample board and wrong in Florida sun, and it is a common miss on otherwise good pools.

Waterline tile deserves its own look. It is seen wet, dry, and almost always at a low angle rather than from above. A tile picked flat on a counter often turns out much darker or much glossier once it is a vertical band at the water.
5. The edge, and where the deck stops

Coping profile is a small decision with an outsized effect on the silhouette. A square-edged, narrow coping makes a pool look contemporary. A heavy rolled bullnose makes the same pool look dated, and it is the single detail most likely to give away a pool's decade.

What the deck meets matters as much as the coping itself. Concrete meeting turf in one clean straight line reads as intentional. Concrete dying into mulch reads as unfinished, and no amount of tile fixes it.
6. The interior finish, and what it actually buys
The finish is priced as a multiplier on the shell rather than as a flat line, so it scales with the size of the pool. The multipliers are in
what a custom pool really costs

What that money changes is the color of the water and the feel underfoot. It does not change the shape. On a well-proportioned pool it is one of the best upgrades available. On a generic one it is a more expensive generic, which is why it sits at number six on this list rather than near the top.

Where it always earns its cost is where the finish is seen dry and close: sun shelves, steps, benches, the top of a spa wall. Those surfaces get inspected at arm's length by everyone who uses the pool. The floor of the deep end does not.
Color is a separate decision from material, and it is the one that changes the read of the water most. What a dark finish does to the color, the heat and the chemistry of a Florida pool is in
dark pool finishes in Florida
7. Shelves, steps and benches are placed, not added

A sun shelf is not an item to add to a list. It is a piece of the plan with a direction, and the direction is the part that gets skipped. It should face where people want to sit in late afternoon, which in most Florida yards is not where the first drawing puts it. A shelf on the wrong side is in full sun at four o'clock and empty by five.

Entry steps work the same way. Steps on the house side are convenient, and they also put the busiest, most visually cluttered part of the pool — handrail, step markers, the change in water color — right in the primary view from the slider. Moving them to a corner is free at layout and impossible afterward.

blog.alt: Pool with a shallow sun shelf holding two white in-water loungers and a raised spa at the far end, on a wide travertine deck that runs toward a lake behind the fence.

children.text: 8. The things you are trying not to see
Two details give a pool away faster than anything on the finish schedule: where the equipment pad sits, and where the returns, skimmer and cleaner line come out.

Walk the sightline from the main slider before the plan is final. Unless someone decides otherwise at layout, the pad and the line routing get placed for plumbing convenience — which is a reasonable default and rarely the same as the view you will look at every day.
Skimmer placement is worth one more minute. Put skimmers where the prevailing wind pushes debris, not where the pipe run is shortest, or you will be netting the same corner for the life of the pool.
9. The night version
The pool is on view from the house every evening, and the night version is the one guests see.

Lighting the water gives you a glowing rectangle in a black yard. Lighting the vertical surfaces gives you depth. Two fixtures aimed to graze a tiled spa wall do more for the view from the slider than six spread evenly around the shell, because the eye reads the lit wall as a back plane and the darkness behind it as distance. The same applies outside the pool: the trunks of the palms behind it, a planting bed, the face of a garden wall.
That makes it a conduit decision more than a fixture decision, and conduit is only cheap while the ground is open and the shell has not been shot. It is on
the pre-excavation list
for that reason.

children.text: Read that table top to bottom: the choices that move the custom read the most are the ones that lock the earliest and cost the most to undo, and they are the cheapest to get right while the drawing is still a drawing.
What does not make a pool look custom
An unusual shape chosen for its own sake.

Freeform costs more per square foot than standard geometry, because curves take longer to form and finish, and a curve that follows nothing in the yard spends that premium on looking dated sooner. A curve that follows something real — a screen wall, a tree you are keeping, the line of the lanai — earns it.
A feature list on a pool with no deck.
Bubblers, fire bowls and a tanning shelf around a pool with three feet of walkway on every side.
The most expensive finish on a stock rectangle.
The finish is the last thing the eye reads, not the first.
A water feature nobody sits near.
A spillway is heard more than it is seen. Put it where people sit, or it is an expense that only shows up in photographs.
If you want the same budget working harder,
the decisions that actually move a Florida pool's price
lays out the trade-offs line by line, and
ten luxury pool designs for Florida homes
shows what these choices look like once they are finished.
Where to start

If you are at the drawing stage rather than the shopping stage, the useful order is: place the pool against the house, then decide the deck, then decide what rises above the water. Everything else can be priced later without moving anything.
Our
gallery of built pools
is the fastest way to work out which of these choices you actually respond to. The
pool cost estimator
shows what each one does to the number, within about 10%. How we run the design stage — site review, layout against the house, then materials — is on the
custom pool and spa construction
page, and if you would rather start with the yard than with a number, a
project estimate
begins with a site visit.

faq.answer: No. A plain rectangle that lines up with the house, has deck where deck is actually used, and carries one element above the waterline will read as custom. A curved shape that follows nothing in the yard usually reads as dated instead, and it costs more per square foot to build.
faq.question: Does a pool have to be an unusual shape to look custom?

faq.answer: Deck proportion, by a wide margin. Widening the side people actually use, and taking deck away from the side nobody walks on, changes how the whole yard reads and costs a fraction of a water feature. It is also decided on the drawing, where it is still free to move.
faq.question: Which choice gives the biggest visual return for the money?

faq.answer: Not as a change order. Anything that rises above the waterline is structural and is designed into the shell, so adding one later means cutting and rebuilding rather than attaching. It is one of the few items on the list that genuinely has to be decided before the steel goes in.
faq.question: Can a raised spa or a raised wall be added after the pool is built?

faq.answer: It changes the color of the water and the feel underfoot, not the shape. On a well-proportioned pool it is one of the better upgrades available; on a generic one it buys a more expensive version of generic. Where it always earns its cost is on the surfaces seen dry and close up, like shelves, steps and the top of a spa wall.
