children.text: A new inground pool in Florida needs one building permit from the city or county that has jurisdiction over your property. That permit covers the pool shell, the deck, the electrical work and the plumbing, each inspected at its own stage, and it is not closed until the safety barrier passes. Depending on your lot, zoning, your HOA, a septic system or a flood zone add approvals of their own. The licensed contractor applies for all of it under their license.
That is the short answer. The rest of this guide explains who issues what, what the plans have to show, what the inspectors look at, and the two things that most often hold a pool permit up.
Who issues pool permits in Florida, and who does not
Florida splits the job in two. The state writes the rules and licenses the people who build; your local government issues the permit and checks the work.
The Florida Building Commission

publishes the Florida Building Code. The 8th Edition (2023) took effect on December 31, 2023, and it is the edition under which current pool permits are reviewed. Residential pools fall under the Residential volume's swimming-pool chapter, which is where barrier, deck, suction-outlet and construction requirements live.
The Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR)

licenses pool and spa contractors through the Construction Industry Licensing Board. A pool built by a licensed contractor is permitted under that license. You can check any license number on the DBPR site; ours are published on every page of this website.
Your city or county building department

receives the application, reviews the plans, issues the permit, performs the inspections and closes the permit. Inside city limits that is usually the city (Gainesville, Ocala); outside, the county (Alachua, Marion). The county you are in decides which portal you use and which local amendments apply.
What the state does not do is issue the permit. There is no statewide pool permit. If a contractor tells you the permit is "handled at the state level," ask again.

blog.alt: Pool with a raised spa and dark tile detail beside a covered patio, with stepping-stone pavers over turf.

children.text: What the building permit application covers
A pool permit application is a package, and the review cannot start until the package is complete. For a custom inground pool it normally includes:
A site plan
showing the lot, the house, the pool and deck footprint, property lines, easements, the equipment pad, and the distance from the pool to each of them.
Engineered pool plans
, sealed by a Florida-licensed engineer, showing the shell, the steel, the depths, the plumbing layout and the equipment.
An electrical plan
for the equipment circuits, the lighting and the bonding grid.
Barrier compliance
, showing how the pool will meet the Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act before the final inspection.
Contractor license and insurance information
for the pool contractor and, where the jurisdiction asks for them, for the electrical and gas subcontractors.
Other sign-offs the lot triggers
: HOA architectural approval where the community requires it, a zoning or setback check, a septic-system review, or a flood-zone elevation review.

Our process front-loads this package. We survey the lot, model the pool against the setbacks and the code in 3D, and get the rendering approved by you before we submit. A clean, complete submission is the single biggest thing a contractor can do to keep the review moving.
Electrical: bonding, GFCI protection and a separate inspection

Pool electrical work is governed by the National Electrical Code's swimming-pool article, which Florida adopts through the Building Code. Two things it requires show up on every residential pool inspection:
Equipotential bonding.

The steel in the shell, the metal in the deck, the pump, the heater and the light niches are all tied into one bonded grid so that nothing around the water can be at a different electrical potential. The inspector wants to see this grid before the deck is poured, because afterwards it is invisible.
Ground-fault protection
on the pool circuits, and defined clearances between the water and outlets, lights and overhead lines.

The electrical scope is permitted under the pool permit or, in some jurisdictions, as its own sub-permit. Either way it has its own rough-in inspection and its own final, by a licensed electrical contractor.
Plumbing and gas

Pool plumbing is inspected under pressure before it is buried. The inspector checks the suction and return runs, the suction outlet (main drain) covers, which must meet the anti-entrapment standard the code references, and any connection to the home's water supply, which needs backflow protection. A gas heater adds a gas line, and the gas work is permitted and inspected as gas work, by a contractor licensed for it.
Zoning, setbacks, easements and the HOA
The building department checks the pool against the Building Code.
Zoning

checks it against your property's rules: how far the pool and the equipment must sit from property lines, whether it can sit in a utility or drainage easement (usually not), and what the lot coverage limits allow. These distances are set by each city or county and vary by zoning district, so there is no statewide setback figure that is worth quoting. Your site plan either passes or needs a variance, and a variance is a separate, slower process.
If you live in a deed-restricted community, the
HOA

architectural review is a separate approval. The building department does not enforce HOA rules, and the HOA does not issue permits, but a project that skips the HOA step can be stopped by the HOA after the permit is issued. We ask for the HOA packet at the first meeting.
Septic systems and wells

This is the item that catches North Florida homeowners most often. Many lots in Alachua, Marion and the surrounding counties are on a septic system rather than sewer. The drainfield and the tank have required separation distances from a pool, and the onsite sewage program (the state agency that regulates septic systems) reviews whether the pool location is acceptable or the system has to be modified. A private well adds its own separation rules. Both are settled before the building permit, not during construction, which is why we locate the tank and drainfield on the first site visit. Our guide to
building a pool in North Florida
covers what else changes on a Gainesville or Ocala lot.

blog.alt: Pool and spa on a stone deck with loungers, overlooking a lake at the rear of the property.

children.text: Flood zones and coastal properties

If any part of the lot is in a FEMA special flood hazard area, the jurisdiction's floodplain rules apply to the pool and, more often, to the equipment pad, which may have to be elevated. Coastal lots can also fall under the state's coastal construction control line, which adds a separate Department of Environmental Protection review. Both are visible on public maps before you design anything, and we check them during the site evaluation.
Safety barriers and the final inspection

Florida's Residential Swimming Pool Safety Act (Chapter 515, Florida Statutes) applies to every new residential pool. Before the pool can pass its final inspection, it must have at least one of the safety features the statute lists. The options include a barrier that meets the Building Code's residential pool barrier requirements, an approved safety pool cover, exit alarms on every door and window with direct access to the pool, and self-closing, self-latching devices on those doors. Most of our clients meet it with a barrier, a screen enclosure, or both.
What the code asks of a barrier, in plain terms:
It must be at least 48 inches high, measured on the outside, with no gaps or footholds that would let a small child climb or pass through.
Gates must open outward, away from the pool, and be self-closing and self-latching, with the latch positioned so a small child cannot reach it.
Where the house wall forms part of the barrier, the doors and windows in that wall have to be protected with alarms or self-closing, self-latching hardware.
A screen enclosure can serve as the barrier when its doors and screens meet the same requirements.

The barrier is checked at the final inspection, which is why a pool that is otherwise finished can sit unused for weeks while a gate latch or a door alarm is corrected. We plan the barrier with the pool, not after it.
The inspection sequence
Inspections are called in by the contractor as each stage is ready, and the next stage cannot be covered until the previous one passes. The order is set by what has to be visible:
Layout and excavation
on some jurisdictions, confirming the pool is where the site plan says.
Steel and plumbing
before the shell is shot: the rebar grid, the bonding, and the plumbing under pressure.
Shell
after the gunite or shotcrete, where required.
Electrical rough-in
before the deck covers the conduit and the bonding connections.
Deck and equipment
as those are completed.
Barrier and final
, including the electrical final, after which the permit is closed.
Each jurisdiction's checklist differs slightly, and some combine stages. The exact list for your address is printed on the permit when it is issued. Our
pool construction timeline guide
shows where each inspection sits inside the build.

blog.alt: Rectangular pool with a raised spa clad in blue tile, set in turf behind a screening hedge.

children.text: The Notice of Commencement and what you sign

For construction above the value threshold set in Florida's construction lien law, a Notice of Commencement is recorded in the county records before the first inspection and a certified copy is posted at the site. It is the document that makes the lien law work for the owner and the people who supply the project, so do not treat it as paperwork. You also sign the permit application as the owner. Read both; we walk you through them.
What slows a pool permit down
In our experience, delays come from a short list and almost never from the review itself:
An incomplete package, usually a missing HOA approval, a site plan without easements, or unsigned engineering.
A septic drainfield or well separation that was discovered after the design was done.
A setback or easement conflict that needs a redesign or a variance.
A barrier plan that was left to the end.

Review times vary by office and by season. We do not publish a number because the honest one changes month to month; ask us what the office covering your address is running at the moment, and we will tell you.
What this means for your project
If you are planning a
custom pool in North Florida

, permitting is part of the build and part of our price, not an extra. We prepare the submittal, pull the permit under our license, coordinate every inspection, and hand you a closed permit at startup. For Gainesville and Alachua County, see our
Gainesville pool builders
page; for Ocala and Marion County, our
Ocala pool builders
page. If you already own a pool and are planning a
complete remodel
, the same process applies to the parts of the work that the code treats as construction.

faq.answer: Yes. An inground pool is a structure with electrical and plumbing systems, and every Florida jurisdiction requires a building permit for it under the Florida Building Code. The permit is applied for at the city or county building department that has authority over your address, not at the state.
faq.question: Do I need a permit to build an inground pool in Florida?

faq.answer: The licensed pool contractor does. The application is made under the contractor's state license, the contractor's engineer seals the plans, and the contractor schedules each inspection. A homeowner can act as owner-builder in Florida, but that route carries the legal responsibility and the inspection coordination, and most pool projects do not use it.
faq.question: Who pulls the pool permit, the homeowner or the contractor?

faq.answer: The jurisdiction can require an after-the-fact permit, inspections of work that is now buried, and corrections to anything that fails. It also surfaces at sale: title and insurance questions about unpermitted work are common. If you are buying a home with a pool, ask the building department for its permit history.
faq.question: What happens if a pool was built without a permit?

faq.answer: Usually, yes, when the work touches structure, plumbing, electrical, equipment or the barrier. Resurfacing alone is treated differently by different jurisdictions. We confirm the scope with the building department before any demolition on a complete pool remodel.

children.text: Upgrade what needs the pool empty, the deck broken out, or the ground open between the pool and the equipment pad. Everything else — the heater, the salt system, the automation, the cleaner, the furniture, the planting — costs about the same next year as it does during the remodel, and does not belong in the fight over this budget.

That is the whole rule, and it is worth stating plainly because most upgrade lists are built the other way around: by walking the yard and naming what would look better. This article does not rank upgrades by how much they improve the pool —
the decisions that make an old pool feel new
does that, item by item. This one sorts the same list by a narrower question: what happens if you say not yet.
Sort by access, not by wish list
Run every line of the proposal past one test. Does this need something open that will be closed when the crew leaves?

children.text: The bottom two rows are where remodel budgets quietly go wrong. They are the easiest items to picture, the easiest to get excited about in a showroom, and the only ones on the list you can genuinely buy on a Saturday two years from now.
What closes when the shell does
Three kinds of item live here, and they close together.
The finish
, because it is the reason the pool was drained in the first place. There is no scope in which it waits.
Anything shaped into the shell

— a bench, a wider entry, a sun shelf, a raised wall. These need the shell cut and re-formed, so they are what stops a job being a resurfacing and makes it a renovation. If your scope was a finish and tile, adding one of them changes the trade list, the schedule and the permit. Which side of that line you are on is the subject of
resurfacing versus a full renovation
, and it is worth knowing before you ask.
Anything that goes through the wall

, which is more than it sounds. A pool light is a niche cast into the wall with conduit back to a junction box, not a lamp; our estimator prices pool LEDs at $450 per fixture, so the count is a line item today and a saw-cut tomorrow. The same applies to where returns point and how many there are. Circulation complaints in an old pool are usually geometry — a corner that stays warm, a spot where leaves collect — and geometry is only cheap to fix while the walls are exposed.

The spa is the largest single item in this group and the one most often postponed by accident. Our estimator prices an integrated spa at $12,000 and a spa with a spillway into the pool at $18,000. Added later it is not an upgrade to a pool; it is a small pool built next to one, with its own excavation, plumbing and finish. If you want it eventually, it belongs in this project.

blog.alt: Rectangular pool with three spillway scuppers set into a rendered wall, a fire bowl on the deck and bougainvillea behind.

children.text: What closes when the deck goes back down

Replacing a deck is usually argued on appearance, which is the weakest version of the argument. The two things a new deck can fix that nothing else can are invisible in the after picture: water that runs away from the house instead of toward it, and the trip step between coping and deck that everyone in the family has learned to step over. Neither is correctable by sealing, and both need the slab out.
So the honest test is not whether the deck looks tired. It is whether it drains and sits flush. If it does, patching and resealing is a legitimate answer and the money is better spent in the shell.

If the slab is coming out anyway, bury what you might want in five years while it is. Conduit at that moment is trenching labor and a length of pipe; after the pour it is a saw cut across a finished surface or an extension cord taped to a wall. Worth sleeving whether or not you commit:
power and low voltage to a future pergola or shade structure;
a circuit, a water line and a drain to wherever an outdoor kitchen would go;
sleeves for the footings of a screen enclosure.
None of them commit you to building anything. They keep the decision cheap, which is the entire point of the list.

blog.alt: Pool with a raised spa on a pale stone deck, with an outdoor shower on the house wall, a dining set and a grill under cover.

children.text: What closes when the trench is filled
The run between the pool and the equipment pad is open for a few days and then not again for years.
Pipe size.
How quietly a modern pump can move water depends on the diameter it is moving it through, and the pipe is under the deck.
Where the pad sits.
Pads end up under bedroom windows because that was the shortest run when the pool was built. Moving one is trenching work, and this is the only moment it is inexpensive.
A gas stub, whether or not you heat this year.
Our estimator prices a heater at $4,500, which is genuinely an any-season purchase — but only if the gas is already there. Stub it and cap it.
Electrical capacity.

Salt chlorination is $2,200 in our estimator and automation $3,500, and both install at the pad later at about the same price, provided the panel and the conduit can carry them. Have that confirmed now, while there is an electrician on site.
What is genuinely fine to leave for later
Failing to defer these is how a remodel budget gets thin in the places that matter.
The heater itself.
Bolt-on equipment. Stub the gas, buy the unit when you want it.
Salt chlorination.
Installs at the pad in an afternoon. No reason for it to compete with the finish.
Automation and controls.
These change faster than anything else in the yard and are the item most likely to be replaced before the plaster is.
A robotic cleaner.
An appliance, not construction.
Furniture and shade.
Decide after living with the new deck layout for a season. Most people place them differently than they planned to.
Planting.
Better done after the machines are gone than dug up twice. If the landscape is in the same project, that is a sequencing conversation, not a scope one.
Rescreening an existing cage.
Independent of all of this — unless the frame itself has to come apart for access, in which case it stops being later and becomes now.

The qualifier at the end of that last line applies to the whole group. Nothing here is deferrable in principle; it is deferrable because it does not need the shell, the slab or the trench. The moment an item needs one of them, it moves up the page regardless of what it is.

blog.alt: Pool in front of a covered lanai with an outdoor kitchen and ceiling fans, a portable basketball hoop at the deck edge and Adirondack chairs to one side.

children.text: Ask for the quote in this order
This is the part that makes the sorting usable, and almost nobody asks for it. Request the itemization grouped by access rather than by trade, so that it reads top to bottom as:
Structural
— shell repairs, steps, bench, ledge, spa
Buried services
— plumbing, gas, conduit, sleeves, drainage
Surfaces
— interior finish, tile, coping, deck
Equipment
— pumps, heater, sanitization, automation
Everything portable
— cleaner, furniture, shade, planting

Quoted that way the list cuts cleanly. If the number comes back high you trim from the bottom, and nothing you remove costs more to add later than it costs today. Quoted by trade — the usual format — the same conversation turns into a redesign, because the item you can safely drop and the item you cannot are tangled in the same row under the same subtotal.

Two things worth asking for alongside it: every rough-in as its own accepted-or-declined line, and the stage each item closes at written beside its price. A sleeve that is a favor does not get laid on a busy morning. A sleeve that is a line item does. The same request on a new build, where the stages are different, is in
the upgrades worth planning before construction begins
One visit or two

The argument for putting everything structural in a single remodel is not that it is tidier. Our estimator adds 8% for difficult access — a narrow side gate, an enclosure that has to come apart, machines that cannot reach the water. A yard carrying that surcharge pays it again on every separate trip back, on top of reopening a deck that was just finished.

That is also the limit of the rule. The items on the defer list do not trigger any of it: a heater, a salt cell or a cleaner arrives through the same gate in someone's hands. Which is exactly why they are on that list and the trench work is not.
If the pile of now items has grown to a new spa, a relocated pad, a full deck replacement and a new ledge, the question has changed from what to upgrade to whether to keep the shell at all —
remodel or rebuild
is where that gets decided, and
what actually changes a remodel's scope
is where the arithmetic sits.
The scope we work through on a
complete pool remodel
follows the same order as the list above. To test the shape of a budget before anyone visits, the
pool cost estimator
uses the figures quoted here and returns a band rather than a price; a
project estimate
starts with someone standing in the yard looking at the deck slope.

cardTitle: What to Upgrade While It's Open

faq.answer: The ones that need the shell, the deck slab or the trench open. Steps, benches, tanning ledges, light niches, extra returns, deck drainage and buried conduit are cheap now and disruptive later. Equipment can be added any year at roughly the same price.
faq.question: If the budget is tight, which upgrades should come first?

faq.answer: The interior finish. It is the reason the pool is drained, so there is no version of the project that leaves it for later. Which grade of finish to choose is a separate question, and it is about years to the next drain rather than about the sample board.
faq.question: Which upgrade cannot be deferred at all?

faq.answer: Yes, but it is structural work rather than a fixture, so it turns a resurfacing into a renovation. Our estimator prices an integrated spa at $12,000 and one with a spillway into the pool at $18,000, before the finish and tile that go with it.
faq.question: Can a spa be added to an existing pool during a remodel?

faq.answer: The case for replacing it is drainage, elevation and the conduit you can bury while it is out, not appearance. If water still runs away from the house and the coping sits flush, patching and resealing is a legitimate answer.
faq.question: Should the deck be replaced if it is still structurally sound?

faq.answer: Scope added after a permit has been issued is generally handled as a revision rather than as part of the original review, which means going back to the reviewer and, depending on what changed, adding an inspection. It is one more reason to settle the structural list before the file goes in.
